articles.title: Australia Draft Bill to Adopt OECD Crypto Tax Reporting Framework
articles.text:
Australia releases draft bill to adopt OECD crypto tax reporting framework
Australia is among 77 jurisdictions committed to adopting CARF, with its first international exchanges of crypto tax data expected in 2028.
Australia has released draft legislation that would enable the automatic exchange of crypto tax information between countries.
The draft bill, Treasury Laws Amendment Bill 2026: Tax information reporting, is open to comment until Oct. 28. It would establish a framework to implement the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) in Australian law and introduce a domestic crypto reporting regime, according to the Australian Treasury.
Australia first signaled its intention to implement CARF in November 2023 and consulted on its proposed approach in late 2024. The government subsequently announced plans to implement both CARF and a domestic crypto reporting regime in its 2025–26 Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook, with international exchanges of crypto tax information expected to begin in 2028.
The OECD approved CARF in August 2022 to address tax evasion risks arising from the growth of crypto assets.
Related: Australia seeks feedback on crypto platform rules ahead of 2027 rollout

articles.title: Scammer Loses $4.8M Stored On Tampered Ledgers: Asia Express
articles.text:
Scammer loses $4.8M stored on tampered Ledgers: Asia Express
A scammer reportedly lost $4.8M of stolen money after storing the funds on tampered Ledgers. Bitcoin and Ether ETFs launch trading in Thailand and South Korea blocks 27 exchanges.
Major irony alert as scammer falls victim to Ledger supply chain attack
Ledger was forced to suspend its reseller network across South East Asia this week, after thieves stole more than $103.4 million from 530 addresses via tampered Ledgers inserted into the supply chain. But in a small measure of poetic justice, one of the “victims” was a scammer themselves according to Chainalysis.
The blockchain monitoring firm reports that the scammer lost 60 Bitcoin, worth about $4.8 million, from three newly purchased Ledgers containing spyware that records seed phrases. The Ledger thieves drained all three of their funds into the same wallet.
In a further irony, the scammer had operated a “task scam” where people were paid to fake sales and reviews of real items. So depending on how much they knew, their victims in turn may not have been entirely honest either. “Then a ‘negative balance’ appeared, and they were told to add their own money in order to get paid,” Chainalysis reports. So it’s possible that a scammer of scammers has just got scammed. In crypto it’s sometimes turtles all the way down.
Despite reports of tampered Ledgers showing up in Europe forcing electronics retailer MediaMarkt to suspend sales, Ledger insists that all of the confirmed thefts to date are from Asia. It has asked resellers in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Hong Kong to remove Ledgers from sale. Trezor too, has decided to shutter some of the more far flung resellers in its network from Jan.1, as it can’t guarantee it can perform the same level of vigilance as it performs on resellers closer to home. There are no reports of tampered Trezors however.
In the midst of the worst hardware wallet scandal since the Coldcard seed phrase debacle at the end of July, Ledger decided it was the ideal moment to launch its latest device. Called Atom, the $849 device combines a crypto wallet with Android apps, which are kept separated from sensitive wallet operations. The device includes protections Ledger says would block the implants used in the Asian thefts and claims it can detect tampering even when switched off.
A first look at Ledger Atom. Source: Ledger
SOUTH KOREA
South Korea moves to block 27 overseas crypto exchanges
South Korean authorities have approved measures to block domestic access to 27 websites operated by unregistered crypto exchanges and other virtual asset service providers, including KuCoin, MEXC, Phemex and Bitrue.
The Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) said in a statement: “With this decision, blocking measures against illegal virtual asset operators will also apply to internet websites, following apps such as those on Apple and Google,” the FIU said, according to a translation.
The list also includes CoinW, BTCC, BitMart, BingX, DigiFinex and others.
South Korea plans cybersecurity overhaul after attacks hit banks, crypto firms
South Korea will tighten cybersecurity requirements for financial institutions after an investigation into earlier security incidents involving 16 companies including crypto exchanges found some big holes.
The Financial Services Commission said it would pursue improved threat monitoring, more frequent security assessments and stronger accountability for executives after an industry-wide review found cybersecurity deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial companies.
South Korean bank launches Bitcoin-backed business loans: Report
Jeonbuk Bank reportedly began offering Bitcoin-backed loans to corporate customers, with a third-party custodian holding the cryptocurrency used as collateral.
THAILAND
Thailand’s Bitcoin, Ether ETFs launch trading
Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission has finalized rules that go into effect Friday allowing crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to list on Thailand’s main stock exchange.
Kicking off with Bitcoin and Ether ETFs, the products must list exclusively on the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Products linked to foreign crypto ETFs will not be permitted initially, and Thai brokers are barred from facilitating investments in overseas crypto ETFs for anyone except institutions and ultra-high-net-worth individuals.
However, James Butterfill, head of research at digital asset investment firm CoinShares, told Cointelegraph not to get too excited.
“I would expect modest inflows initially, with tens of millions of US dollars across the first products a more realistic starting expectation than billions,” he said.
AUSTRALIA
Australia seeks feedback on crypto platform rules ahead of 2027 rollout
Australia’s securities regulator opened consultation Thursday on proposed capital, custody and trading requirements for crypto platforms, as it prepares to implement legislation passed in April that expands oversight of the industry.
The proposals include three alternative capital models, restrictions on platforms trading for their own account and quarterly reporting of wallets holding customer assets. ASIC also proposes allowing offshore custody while seeking feedback on safeguards if an overseas parent or related company fails.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) also proposed expanding the rules for contracts for difference (CFDs) to crypto. CFDs let traders bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset.
CHINA
Chinese fraud victims lose key court battle over 61,000 Bitcoin
Chinese fraud victims seeking to recover 61,000 Bitcoin seized by the British government have lost a key legal battle after London’s High Court ruled that Chinese law, rather than English law, should govern claims to the assets.
“The relevant damage occurred in China. The Applicants parted with their money in China,” Justice Mark Turner wrote. “The contractual relationships thereby induced were entered into in China.”
The dispute stems from an investment fraud scheme orchestrated by Zhimin Qian between 2014 and 2017, with British authorities seizing the assets during a money-laundering investigation. The claimants will appeal the ruling in British courts.
THE PHILIPPINES
Coins.ph says it still has a Philippine central bank license intact despite reports
Coins.ph said it is still licensed by the country’s central bank despite reports that it could face license revocation over alleged transactions involving restricted offshore gambling operators.
Coins.ph is one of the largest crypto exchanges in the Philippines, and the reported license risk follows restrictions imposed by the central bank on some incoming transfers involving DCPay Philippines which operates Coins.ph’s peso e-wallet services.
“Coins.ph firmly denies any claim that it knowingly serves offshore gaming or gambling operators,” the company said. “Our users’ funds are safe; we continue to operate as a BSP-licensed institution,” it added.
HONG KONG
Binance may add Asian stocks to the platform
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said during Token2049 the exchange may add Hong Kong, Korean, Taiwanese and Brazilian equities to its platform.
Second Solana ETF lists in Hong Kong
Pando Finance’s Solana ETF has launched in Hong Kong’s HKEX under the ticker 2831.hk. It’s the second such fund and has a 0.6% fee, undercutting the first fund from ChinaAMC which charges 0.99% annually.
SINGAPORE
Singapore crypto scam losses fall by 43%
A crackdown by Singapore Police in partnership with local crypto exchanges helped contribute to a 43% fall in reported losses from crypto scams year over year.
Revolut to open new Singapore office
Revolut has announced it will open a new Singapore office, invest S$350 million (US$273M) over the next five years, and expand its local workforce from 170 to 300

articles.title: Binance.US Pursues $1B Valuation After $100M Funding Round: Report
articles.text:
Binance.US seeks $1B valuation in potential $100M funding round: Report
The crypto exchange was reportedly looking to use the additional funding to regain market share following Binance’s 2023 settlement with US authorities.
Binance.US is reportedly seeking to raise up to $100 million in a funding round that could value the cryptocurrency exchange at $1 billion.
According to a Thursday Bloomberg report, the US-based crypto exchange is pursuing private investment as it looks to expand its business. The potential $1 billion valuation would be well below the $4.5 billion pre-money valuation it secured in 2022, when it raised $200 million in seed funding.
Binance.US reportedly informed World Liberty Financial, the crypto platform co-founded by US President Donald Trump and his sons, about the funding round, but the company will not be participating. Last year, Binance was embroiled in a controversial $2 billion investment between an entity tied to the United Arab Emirates royalty and World Liberty using the platform’s USD1 stablecoin.
The proposed funding round is reportedly part of Binance.US’ efforts to regain market share against larger rivals following a 2023 settlement between Binance Holdings Ltd. and US authorities. As part of the agreement, Binance Holdings agreed to pay $4.3 billion in penalties and accept additional monitoring and oversight, while its then-CEO, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty to a felony charge. Zhao completed a four-month sentence in prison before receiving a pardon from Trump in 2025.
Related: Binance says employees questioned in UAE cleared and released

articles.title: Crypto Today: Bo Hines, Ledger Wallet, Australia Rules
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, a Wall Street Journal investigation revealed that former Trump crypto adviser Bo Hines retained a financial stake in a firm that benefited from a Tether deal while he helped advance US stablecoin legislation. Meanwhile, Ledger introduced an $849 hardware wallet with stronger anti-tampering protections following a security incident in Asia, and Australia’s securities regulator proposed new capital, custody and trading requirements for crypto platforms ahead of a 2027 rollout.
Former Trump adviser retained stake in firm that benefited from stablecoin law
Former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines retained a one-third stake in an investment firm that received millions of dollars from Tether while he was helping advance landmark US stablecoin legislation, according to a Wall Street Journal investigation.
The report found that Nxum, an investment company Hines co-founded, received $6.3 million through an agreement with Tether, with the first payment arriving while Hines was still serving in the Trump administration.
Hines reportedly remained in contact with Nxum partners through Signal, sharing updates on the GENIUS Act and encouraging them to criticize Republican lawmakers who opposed the legislation.
The GENIUS Act, which established a federal regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, was signed into law in July 2025. Hines left the administration shortly afterward, joining Tether as a strategic adviser in August before becoming CEO of its US operations.
The revelations add to scrutiny of financial ties between Trump administration officials and the cryptocurrency industry. Several former regulators have also moved into senior industry positions, including former CFTC Commissioner Summer Mersinger, who became CEO of the Blockchain Association.
Ledger’s answer to wallet tampering costs $849 and ships next year
Ledger unveiled a new device on Thursday with stronger protections against tampering, days after confirming that wallets sold through a reseller in Asia contained malicious implants.
The French hardware wallet maker introduced Atom, an $849 device that combines a crypto wallet with everyday apps through a smartphone-like design. Atom separates Android apps from sensitive wallet operations and includes protections Ledger says would block the implants used in the recent Asia incident. It’s also advertised to detect tampering even when switched off.
The company expects to begin shipping the device in summer 2027, according to an announcement shared with Cointelegraph.
Ledger said Atom will also support AI agent approvals, encrypted messaging and post-quantum cryptography.
The announcement follows a security incident that surfaced on Friday involving malicious implants found in wallets sold through authorized reseller CryptoBilis. Ledger has requested that distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong suspend sales of its products. European retail chain MediaMarkt has also pulled Ledger wallets off its shelves.
Australia seeks feedback on crypto platform rules ahead of 2027 rollout
Australia’s securities regulator opened consultation Thursday on proposed capital, custody and trading requirements for crypto platforms, as it prepares to implement legislation passed in April that expands oversight of the industry.
The proposals include three alternative capital models, restrictions on platforms trading for their own account and quarterly reporting of wallets holding customer assets. ASIC also proposes allowing offshore custody while seeking feedback on safeguards if an overseas parent or related company fails.
“Our proposed guidance and standards acknowledge the increasing role of digital assets and tokenization, including in traditional parts of the financial system,” said ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland.
The proposed guidance and standards would give crypto operators greater clarity on requirements to obtain a license, safeguard customer assets and meet financial requirements under the new framework. The consultation follows Parliament’s passage of the Corporations Amendment (Digital Assets Framework) Act earlier this year.

articles.title: White House Crypto Adviser’s Company Financially Benefitted from GENIUS Act: WSJ
articles.text:
Ex-Trump crypto adviser profited after helping pass stablecoin bill: WSJ
The Wall Street Journal reported that a company co-founded by Bo Hines benefited from the passage of the GENIUS stablecoin bill.
Bo Hines, previously a crypto adviser to US President Donald Trump who later joined stablecoin issuer Tether, reportedly kept a stake in a company that profited from the passage of a stablecoin bill when he was still at the White House.
According to a Wednesday report from The Wall Street Journal, Hines had a one-third stake in the investment company he co-founded, Nxum, while pushing US lawmakers to pass the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins, or GENIUS, Act. The legislation reportedly came amid Nxum receiving $6.3 million as part of a deal with stablecoin issuer Tether, behind the USDt (USDT) token, with the first payment going through while Hines was still serving in government.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Hines kept in contact with his partners at Nxum, updating them on progress with the GENIUS Act through the Signal app while serving as Trump’s crypto adviser.
He also reportedly pressed the Nxum partners to label any Republican lawmakers opposing the stablecoin bill as “undermining the president” and “bought and paid for by democratic shills like Coinbase and a16z.” Hines joined Tether as a “strategic adviser” in August 2025, becoming CEO of its US arm the following month.
The reported deal between a former White House official and a crypto company continues to shine a spotlight on accusations that Trump and his family and staff are personally benefitting from laws they help to draft and pass. The president disclosed earning $1.4 billion from investments tied to digital assets in 2025, which included millions of dollars from his family’s crypto company World Liberty Financial, behind the issuance of the USD1 stablecoin.
Related: EU lawmakers push crypto onto anti-corruption agenda
The GENIUS Act passed Congress and was signed into law in July 2025 in a ceremony attended by many cryptocurrency executives, including those behind stablecoins like Tether and Circle. Hines was in attendance and personally recognized by Trump at the event.
Though it was signed into law in 2025, the GENIUS stablecoin bill requires rules from government agencies overseeing the tokens, including the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Federal Reserve Board and Treasury Department. The law is scheduled to go into effect in January 2027.
Cointelegraph reached out to Tether for comment on the accusations in the report but did not receive an immediate response.
‘Revolving door’ of US policymakers to crypto companies continues
Several figures previously in government have left to become executives or advisers to digital asset companies. In addition to Hines joining Tether, Summer Mersinger, a former commissioner with the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), resigned her position three years before her term was scheduled to end for a position as CEO of the crypto advocacy group Blockchain Association.
On Wednesday, Solidus Labs announced that Kevin Webb, a former CFTC senior counsel and adviser to former Commissioner Brian Quintenz, would join the fintech company as its vice president of policy. Webb isn’t the first former commissioner at the company, as the CFTC’s Dawn Stump left the agency in 2022 to join Solidus as a “strategic adviser.”
Magazine: Can the SEC and CFTC’s pro-crypto rules be overturned? Legal opinion

articles.title: Mastercard Launches Stablecoin Global Money Platform With BVNK
articles.text:
Mastercard brings stablecoin balances into traditional banking and card payments
The launch of Global Money Platform marks Mastercard’s first major integration with BVNK since its August acquisition, with Nuvei and Marqeta among the first companies to adopt the platform.
Mastercard is expanding its role in stablecoin payments with a new platform that lets businesses integrate digital currencies into traditional banking and card services, a move that could make it easier for companies to offer stablecoin payments without building their own infrastructure.
The service, dubbed Global Money Platform, is Mastercard’s first major integration with BVNK since it acquired the stablecoin infrastructure company in August, the payments giant announced Thursday.
According to Mastercard, businesses can use the platform to hold and convert fiat currencies and stablecoins, offer stablecoin-linked cards and make payments directly from stablecoin balances into recipients’ local bank accounts.
The service connects to Mastercard Move, the company’s global money transfer network, which can route payments to more than 17 billion destinations, including bank accounts and cards. It also connects stablecoin balances to Mastercard’s merchant network, allowing customers to spend them with payment cards. Nuvei, Marqeta and several other fintech companies are among the first integration partners.
The launch extends Mastercard’s role beyond processing payments to providing infrastructure that financial companies can use to offer stablecoin services under their own brands. It also puts Mastercard in closer competition with Visa, which launched a platform in July that lets financial institutions hold, mint, and transfer stablecoins.
It comes as research from Standard Chartered points to growing stablecoin transaction activity, even as the circulating supplies of major tokens such as USDt and USDC have remained relatively flat this year.
Related: US accounting overhaul could make stablecoins more attractive to corporations: Tempo

articles.title: Sweden’s Riksbank Recommends Digital Krona Preparations
articles.text:
Sweden revisits digital krona as ECB advances digital euro plans
Sweden’s Riksbank has recommended that lawmakers prepare for a possible digital krona, citing concerns over foreign-currency stablecoins and the future of domestic payments.
Sweden’s central bank is revisiting the possibility of introducing a digital krona, citing the European Central Bank’s (ECB) progress toward a digital euro and the growing use of stablecoins as reasons to reconsider a central bank digital currency (CBDC).
In an Oct. 7 letter to parliament’s Finance Committee, published Thursday, the Riksbank urged lawmakers to begin preparing legislation for a potential digital krona, three years after a government inquiry concluded there was insufficient need for one.
The letter pointed to the ECB’s planned digital euro pilot in 2027 and a potential public launch in 2029. According to the Riksbank, Sweden’s payment system could become less competitive without a comparable digital version of its own currency.
The central bank also identified the growing use of foreign-currency stablecoins, particularly those pegged to the US dollar, as a longer-term concern, though it sees the near-term risk as limited.
“If stablecoins pegged to foreign currencies are considered attractive as a means of payment, the use of the Swedish krona could come under pressure even within Sweden’s borders,” the letter read.
The Riksbank estimates that introducing a digital krona would take at least five years, excluding the time required for legislative changes. For this reason, it recommends beginning legal preparations now, even if Sweden ultimately decides against launching a CBDC.
Related: AllUnity debuts SEKAU, a fully reserved Swedish krona stablecoin

articles.title: Bitcoin Risks Sub-$80,000 ‘Volatile Retest’ After US PPI Overshoot
articles.text:
Bitcoin slips under $80K after US PPI gains most in four years
BTC buyers attempted to defend $80,000 support after September US producer inflation overshot expectations by 100 basis points for the largest monthly gain since March 2022
Bitcoin (BTC) dipped below $80,000 on Thursday as US Producer Price Index (PPI) data significantly beat expectations.
Key points:
- Bitcoin briefly traded below $80,000 on the back of a 100-basis-point overshoot in US PPI inflation data.
- September PPI measured 6.3% against market expectations of 5.3%, the biggest monthly jump since March 2022.
- BTC price analysis saw the potential for a “volatile retest” of trend lines around $78,000 next.
Biggest PPI increase since March 2022 adds to Bitcoin tailwinds
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD slipping to its lowest levels since Sept. 18, declining as much as 1.8% on the day, before rebounding to around $81,000.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
September PPI came in at 6.3%, a full 100 basis points above its anticipated level, while core PPI rose to 5% versus an expected 4.4%, per data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
“The September increase is the largest advance since rising 1.7% in March 2022. On an unadjusted basis, the index for final demand climbed 6.3% for the 12 months ended in September, the largest 12-month increase since moving up 6.4% in December 2022,” an official news release confirmed.
US PPI one-month % change. Source: BLS
The numbers come a day after the Consumer Price Index (CPI) also overshot estimates, causing crypto and risk assets to fall. Risk assets were already under pressure from a tech sell-off centered in South Korea, where the KOSPI Composite Index fell 7.5% on Thursday.
Economist Mohamed El-Erian described PPI as “even more striking” than the CPI result. El-Erian and others noted that US bond yields were not rising on the back of higher inflation numbers. The US 10-year bond yield was down almost 3% at the time of writing, at its lowest levels since Sept. 23.
US 10-year bond yield one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Robin Brooks, former chief FX strategist at Goldman Sachs, repeated earlier findings which suggested that yields had “decoupled” from US macro data as market priorities switched to the government’s handling of the federal budget deficit.
Brooks compared the 30-day correlation between upside data surprises and daily moves in the 10-year yield, and revealed that it had dropped from near 0.6 earlier in 2026 to just below zero as of the end of August.
“That indicates that yields have decoupled from data and the obvious explanation for this is that markets are more focused on the trajectory of the deficit, so they’re pushing up longer-term yields regardless of what data surprises are doing,” he summarized in a blog post last month.
Analysis eyes “early-stage bull market” support retest
BTC price action meanwhile brought two support trend lines back into focus: the 21-week and 50-week exponential moving averages (EMA) at $76,144 and $78.459, respectively.
Related: CryptoQuant’s 3 charts keeping Bitcoin’s ‘Uptober’ thesis valid
Trader and analyst Rekt Capital noted that BTC/USD could still retest both and preserve its overall bullish trend.
“Deviating below them on a volatile retest to find a pullback bottom has historically happened in early-stage Bull Markets. These deviations however would occur after a bullish crossovers of these two EMAs, whereas Bitcoin is still pre-crossover,” Rekt Capital said in an X post.
BTC/USD one-week chart. Source: Rekt Capital on X.com
Bitcoin remained below the area between $82,500 and $82,800, a key support zone of interest in recent weeks.
Analyst Aksel Kibar said that Bitcoin’s latest weekly close around $83,700 lacked strength as a breakout.
“A weekly close inside the range can resume wide consolidation between 60K-82.8K 75K can be utilized as the pattern (rectangle bottom reversal) negation level,” he said.

articles.title: Russia to Ban P2P Crypto Trades, Block Self-Custody Transfers
articles.text:
Russia to ban direct peer-to-peer crypto trades starting July 2027
Russia plans to ban direct P2P crypto trades from July 1, 2027, while separate rules already prohibit transfers from digital accounts to self-custody wallets.
Russia will ban direct peer-to-peer (P2P) cryptocurrency transactions between individuals starting next year, requiring individuals to use authorized intermediaries for such trades.
The restriction will end individuals’ ability to exchange crypto assets directly without intermediaries, the Bank of Russia, the country’s central bank, explained in guidance updated Monday. The regulator confirmed that such transactions will remain permitted only until July 1, 2027.
The regulator also clarified that individuals are not allowed to transfer crypto assets from their digital accounts to their own non-custodial, or self-custodial, wallets.
The move comes as Russia expands its regulated crypto market. On Monday, the Bank of Russia authorized Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to offer crypto exchange services after earlier approving it as a digital asset custodian.
The approval follows Russia’s new crypto rules, which came into force on Sept. 1 and brought exchange operators and custodians under central bank oversight. The country also continues to prohibit cryptocurrency payments for goods and services.
Industry executives have previously told Cointelegraph that restrictions on P2P crypto trading and noncustodial wallets may be difficult to enforce. Jan3 CEO Samson Mow said P2P trading is more resilient to regulatory crackdowns than centralized platforms, while SatoshiLabs executive Stepan Uherik said wallet app bans would leave hardware and desktop wallets unaffected.
Related: Russia clears first crypto exchanges, custodians under new law

articles.title: Nasdaq-listed Tron Sets up $200M ATM Share Offering for TRX Acquisitions
articles.text:
Nasdaq-listed Tron sets up $200M ATM share offering to fuel TRX acquisitions
The Nasdaq-listed treasury company holds about $237 million in TRX tokens and plans to raise additional capital to fund its purchases, alongside its daily accumulation.
Nasdaq-listed Tron (TRON) has filed for a new at-the-market (ATM) share offering allowing it to sell up to $200 million of common stock that will fund an even-larger Tron (TRX) treasury.
The deal allows Tron to periodically sell shares of its common stock at $0.0001 par value through Clear Street, which acts as an agent and retains a commission of up to 3% of gross proceeds, according to a Wednesday filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The company’s existing TRX accumulation program, announced in February, called for the purchase of approximately $50,000 worth of TRX per day for 360 consecutive days. Tron’s treasury holds 718.9 million TRX tokens, currently worth about $237 million, after the company’s latest acquisition of 149,369 TRX at an average price of $0.3347 on Thursday.
Tron SEC filing on a $200 million ATM program with Clear Street LLC. Source: sec.gov
The company’s shares opened 4.7% lower on Thursday, poised to extend their roughlly 67% 12-month decline, according to Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Hidden Text, a Fake Mailbox: How Researchers Got Rogue AI Agents to Talk - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Swarmchasers used hidden text and a mailbox to exchange messages with some AI agents while they were still running; one described its job as checking public Amap map data.
- The fleet made more than 2,600 attempts to retrieve Amap data, and some agents tried anti-bot workarounds or used exposed API credentials.
- The activity traced to Tencent Cloud, but a person close to Tencent said the project tested third-party models rather than Hunyuan.
Researchers investigating AI agents hijacking Alibaba’s mapping service, Amap, managed to talk directly to some while the software was still running.
To do so, they added text invisible to human readers but visible to web-reading tools to a report the agents appeared to be scanning, then used a mailbox to ask about their tasks and environment.
One agent said it was checking a map fact—how many entrance labels appeared for a scenic spot on Amap—and described itself as running in a restricted Tencent Cloud sandbox. The researchers could not independently establish which model powered each run. They called it the first outside communication with an active rogue-agent fleet they knew of.
The October 14 Swarmchasers report traced more than 2,600 attempts from September 28 to October 8 to retrieve data from Amap, a Chinese mapping app operated by Alibaba. Some tasks were mundane, such as checking which entrance visitors most often use for Chengdu Zoo. Some agents kept trying after the service blocked their requests.
The researchers’ hidden text falsely described the mailbox as an AI service with computer-use abilities. In reality, it routed messages to a Claude agent operated by the researchers, which could use a debugging browser. The exchanges were not a controlled test, and the researchers’ intervention may have affected what agents said.
After Amap blocked requests, some agents tried to intercept tokens generated by anti-bot software, route traffic through third-party page readers, or use API credentials exposed in public code repositories. One exposed key-and-security-code pair returned real place data. Researchers also found requests targeting four development or pre-production hosts, but said they had no evidence the agents accessed private systems.
Public records linked the fleet to Tencent Cloud since all 17 inboxes the researchers inspected were created from Tencent servers in Hong Kong, and observed direct requests passed through a proxy called hysandbox-ats. A person close to Tencent told Swarmchasers the activity came from a temporary evaluation project testing third-party AI models, not Tencent’s Hunyuan models.
That said, this is not the first time we hear of malicious AI agents. OpenAI-powered AI agents have gone a lot further. Back in September OpenAI revealed that some of its agents had probed Hugging Face weeks before the July breach, and a separate investigation found roughly 1,200 agents coordinating on an internal message board, with about 700 joining the attack. Meta and Anthropic also revealed similar incidents of rogue AI agents escaping sandboxed environments.
Another report linked OpenAI agents to breaches of four additional platforms, but Swarmchasers found no evidence that the Tencent-linked agents coordinated with one another in real time.
The last observed activity from the fleet was on October 8. The researchers said Tencent’s internal review, as described by their source, found no evidence that the agents had been coordinated to target a specific platform or had breached external systems.

articles.title: Can The SEC And CFTC’s Pro-Crypto Rules Be Overturned? Legal Opinion
articles.text:
Can the SEC and CFTC’s pro-crypto rules be overturned? Legal opinion
The SEC and the CFTC have issued a raft of pro-crypto rules recently. But will the rules hold up in court, and can they be easily rolled back by the “anti-crypto army”?
In the wake of the failed CLARITY cloture vote in the Senate, the SEC and CFTC immediately moved to issue their own rules for crypto markets.
Two days after the vote, the SEC unveiled a five-year exemption that permits the issuing and trading of stock tokens. OXK has since teamed up with ICE to launch trading in 63 NYSE-listed stocks and Securitize launched 12 Securitize Stocks, including Apple, Nvidia and Microsoft.
The SEC has also issued guidance clarifying that a crypto token doesn’t become a security just because a project is buying back its own tokens, and stated that liquid staking tokens are not securities. It has also proposed new rules for the custody of crypto assets.
The CFTC, meanwhile, moved to exempt some crypto software providers from registration requirements. It has proposed a new “crypto asset market” registration category and intends to allow registered exchanges to offer leveraged trading.
But the concern among some in the industry is that these rules could be built on shifting sands. TD Cowen has cautioned that agency rules “are the easiest to rescind” — which was demonstrated when Trump-appointed commissioners wiped away all traces of the Gary Gensler era.
A 2024 Supreme Court decision also means agency rules can more easily be overturned by the courts. 
The durability of regulator rulemaking is currently being tested in court, with a community bank group suing the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for exceeding its authority by allowing crypto firms to obtain national trust bank charters.
To discuss the legal issues involved, Magazine spoke with Yuriy Brisov from D&A Partners. This is an edited version of the conversation.
Magazine: SEC Chair Paul Atkins said after the CLARITY vote failed that the agency was releasing rules because Congress didn’t. Are agencies like the SEC supposed to create rules, or are they just supposed to interpret rules that already exist?
Brisov: They are supposed to create rules. They have this power under the Exchange Act of 1934. The SEC was created as a result of the major meltdown in the US markets in the end of the 1920s. From the moment of creation, the SEC had the power to create rules and regulations on how the laws should apply. American legislation works by creating general rules, like a frame, and then it has a watchdog watching over these regulations. 
There was a reason why it was created like this — so that when, say, blockchain tokens came along, the US legislation would be ready to accommodate new technology. That’s what the Commission has been doing for ages now, and it’s obviously within their powers.
Magazine: Can they interpret the rules in the opposite way to an SEC appointed by a previous administration?
Brisov: There should be a reason for that. They can, in theory, do that, but it should be all within the formation of the body of law. Under Gary Gensler, the Commission tried to apply these rules to tokens. It turns out that it failed because there is still vagueness, and many companies left the US market for good.
This is the opening for the new Commission to oversee these rules and say, “You tried, but we can see that it’s not working. So we’ll offer our own rules.” But the power to offer rules is limited. If they offer some regulations that would lay an unbearable economic burden on companies, or something bizarre, there are also laws that allow companies or any damaged party to challenge this regulation in court and say, “We don’t like what the SEC has been doing because it’s damaging the market.”
In 2011, there was a case when the SEC applied new rules on how shareholders vote through a proxy. And the business community said, “it’s bizarre, it’s burdensome, and we don’t like it.” There was a case, Business Roundtable vs SEC, and [business] won.
Magazine: What was the Chevron decision by the Supreme Court and how does its overturning in 2024 impact court cases about rulemaking by agencies like the SEC and CFTC?
Brisov: Chevron was a famous case of 1984. The court basically said that if the law is vague or there are uncertainties and ambiguities in the statute, then we should use the agency’s interpretation as the law. In June 2024, Loper Bright was a new precedent that overruled Chevron. It’s now saying that we don’t have to. Of course, [the SEC is] a strong authority: Who knows securities laws better than the SEC? But the court should use its own brains and apply the Howey case itself.
Magazine: So that makes it more likely that SEC rules could be overturned?
Brisov: In some cases, the courts can come up with a different conclusion.
You cannot just come and say “we don’t like this regulation.” For instance, if you’re a traditional broker-dealer or traditional participant of the investment market in the United States and you say, ‘Look, I’m suffering because of this new regulation’ they should be able to prove that there was not enough research and that it’s burdensome for the business, and it’s not profitable for the US market. If they prove damages and if they prove a lack of research, then the court can overrule this regulation.
From what I can see, Paul Atkins and the SEC have been consulting with many crypto firms, with VCs. They’ve been doing their research, so it’s not something they just came up with within a day.
Related: OKX, NYSE parent file to launch tokenized US stock platform
Magazine: Let’s assume the SEC and CFTC rules survive for the next two years, and businesses invest a lot of money into infrastructure around tokenized stocks based on the new rules. Could a new SEC unilaterally reverse the rules or do they have to take into account the businesses built on top of the old interpretation?
Brisov: They have to take them into account. If there is the potential for the US market to grow and to benefit from this regulation, they won’t be able to just overrule it. There is the same thought process that either an agency or a court goes through. It’s called IRAC: issue, rule, analysis, conclusion. They would have to apply understandable, transparent logic.
They can’t just say we don’t like it. They have to explain. They have to bring up an economic background for it. They have to bring up research, and they have to prove that it’s insufficient. And only then can they come to a different conclusion. 
For the sake of argument, we could say that Paul Atkins hates the Howey test, and he would have been happy just to abandon it — but he can’t do it. In every note, he keeps repeating that the Howey case still works, it’s still a valid regulation in the United States. However, we can interpret it in this case, and this case, differently — and this is our logic. This is what allows us to do that, and he explains it transparently. 
Magazine: The SEC appears to have been working on the innovation exemption for years. But the SEC more recently came up with an FAQ saying that a crypto company buying back its own token does not make a commodity token a security. Could I be secure and comfortable launching a token buyback scheme on the basis of an FAQ by the SEC?
Brisov: If you follow it, and it’s created by the people who know what they’re saying, probably you will be in the clear. But it’s not legislation. An FAQ is just like a manual. It doesn’t have any authority, even for the staff.
Magazine: So the FAQ isn’t saying they changed the rules; it is just saying this is what the rules are?
Brisov: It’s just some extra explanation, like a casebook in the university. They are staff notes. A manual that explains for the staff how they should work and how they should understand this. They rewrite them quite often.
Magazine: They rewrote the FAQ after a week because a16z’s legal counsel said it left a massive loophole.
Brisov: Exactly, and that’s how it should be done. It’s not regulation or legislation, they can change them every week.

articles.title: HEX Token Erases $160M Following Reports of Founder Richard Schueler’s Arrest
articles.text:
HEX token sellers erase $160M following reports of founder Richard Schueler arrest
The HEX token’s price declined by 30% following local media reports of the Istanbul arrest of founder Richard Schueler, nearly two years after Interpol issued a “Red Notice.”
The Hex (HEX) token fell nearly 30% in the past 24 hours after local media reports of founder Richard Schueler, also known as Richard Heart, being detained by authorities in Istanbul.
The HEX token declined to $0.0006 as of 11:28 am UTC on Thursday, erasing about $160 million from its market capitalization, from more than $500 million on Wednesday to $340 million by press time, according to CoinMarketCap. It previously topped $0.44 in September 2021.
On Wednesday, news outlet Ihlas Haber Ajansı (IHA) reported that Schueler and his wife were detained in Istanbul by Turkish authorities. Police reportedly seized multiple devices, hardware wallets, jewelry and handguns.
The reported arrest comes nearly two years after the world’s largest international police organization, Interpol, issued a “Red Notice” for Schueler for allegedly committing tax fraud and assault, with Finnish authorities seeking his arrest.
A spokesperson for Finland’s National Bureau of Investigations declined to comment on the matter.
Schueler was also listed on Europe’s most wanted fugitives list on similar allegations, claiming that he “physically assaulted a 16-year-old victim by grabbing their hair, dragging them into the stairwell and knocking them to the ground.”
In July 2023, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) sued Schueler, alleging he raised $1 billion in an unregistered securities offering and misappropriated at least $12 million.
US District Judge Carol Bagley Amon dismissed the case in February 2025, after ruling that the activities were not sufficiently directed at US investors. In April 2025, the SEC said it didn’t intend to refile its securities fraud complaint against Schueler.

articles.title: Google Says It Just Cracked One of Quantum Computing's Biggest Bottlenecks - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Google Quantum AI said Thursday that a technique called magic state cultivation cut errors about 40-fold on its Willow chip, producing magic states with 99.99% fidelity.
- Magic states are single-use resources needed to run useful quantum programs, and Google says some estimates put the cost of making them at up to 95% of a quantum computer's capacity.
- Cultivation is one of the tricks behind Google's 2025 estimate that RSA-2048 encryption could fall to under a million noisy qubits, though code-breaking would need magic states with errors near one in 10 billion.
Google says it has turned one of quantum computing's most promising paper tricks into something that actually works on a chip.
In a paper published in Science on Thursday, the company's Quantum AI team showed that a technique called magic state cultivation cut errors by about 40 times on its Willow processor.
Making quantum computers cheaper to build matters far beyond physics labs, because it brings forward the day they do useful work, like designing drugs and new materials, and also the day one could break the encryption that protects bank logins and Bitcoin wallets.
Quantum computers run on qubits—quantum bits that can hold a blend of 0 and 1 at once, letting them explore many answers in parallel. They are also absurdly fragile: a little heat or electrical noise can flip a qubit and wreck a calculation, which is why the whole industry is obsessed with error correction (spreading one piece of information across many qubits so mistakes can be caught and fixed).
Error correction handles the simple operations well, but a genuinely useful program also needs a class of harder operations that can't be protected the same way. To run them, the machine first has to manufacture magic states, which work like single-use fuel cells for those operations: each one is consumed the moment it's used.
Producing clean magic states has always been brutally expensive. Some estimates put the bill at up to 95% of a quantum computer's entire capacity, according to Google, leaving very little room for the actual computing.
Physicists Sergei Bravyi and Alexei Kitaev laid out the standard fix in 2004 with magic state distillation, which takes many noisy magic states and boils them down into a few clean ones. It works, but it demands sprawling qubit "factories" that do nothing else.
In 2024, Google researchers proposed a cheaper route they named magic state cultivation. Instead of a factory, this technique behaves like a filter, injecting a rough magic state into a tiny patch of the chip to then run a chain of checks on it, throw out every attempt with a detected flaw, and keep growing the survivors. Their paper went as far as suggesting further distillation "may never be needed in practice."
“On Google Quantum AI's Willow processor, our protocol achieved an extraordinary 40-fold reduction in errors relative to un-cultivated states. And we got T-states with a record logical fidelity of 99.99%,” Google said.
Only about 8% of attempts passed every check, meaning the chip discards more than nine out of every 10 tries to keep one clean state.
Cultivation is one of the tricks behind Gidney's 2025 estimate that RSA-2048 encryption could be broken with under a million noisy qubits, a 20-fold drop from the 20 million he estimated in 2019. Until this experiment, cultivation had only been tested in theory and computer simulations.
Google kept tightening the screws in March, when a Quantum AI whitepaper co-authored with Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake and Stanford cryptographer Dan Boneh put the cost of breaking Bitcoin's elliptic curve cryptography (the math that stops anyone from deriving your private key from your public address) at fewer than 500,000 physical qubits. That follows the company's Quantum Echoes experiment last October, the first verified quantum speedup on real hardware.
Nobody is draining wallets with this. The experiment used at most 54 of Willow's 105 qubits, and the paper notes that factoring an RSA-2048 key would require magic states with errors around one in 10 billion, roughly a million times cleaner than what Google just achieved.
Google says the next step is running cultivation at a larger scale. The team projects that halving Willow's underlying hardware noise would push magic state errors down to about two in 100,000, because errors in the process shrink with the cube of the chip's noise level.

articles.title: Russia Will Soon Ban Peer-to-Peer Bitcoin Trading, Central Bank Confirms - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- The Bank of Russia confirmed in an October 12 FAQ that direct crypto trades between individuals are legal only until July 1, 2027, citing new law.
- The regulator also says individuals cannot move crypto from a digital account to their own non-custodial wallet or transfer it to another person through depository-run addresses.
- Sberbank joined the central bank's crypto exchange register on October 12 and plans to launch its first crypto products on December 1.
Russians have a little over eight months left to trade Bitcoin and other crypto directly with each other. From July 1, 2027, peer-to-peer deals—where two people swap rubles for coins without a regulated middleman—will no longer be legal, the Bank of Russia confirmed this week.
The clarification sits in updated guidance the regulator posted on its official website on October 12.
The legal basis is Federal Law No. 282-FZ, “On Digital Currencies and Digital Rights,” which President Vladimir Putin signed on August 4 and which took effect September 1. Article 30 lists the crypto operations residents may carry out without a licensed intermediary, and from July 2027 that list no longer includes trades between individuals.
From that date, residents may only trade crypto through, or directly with, companies that “organize the circulation” of digital currencies—mainly brokers licensed by the Bank of Russia and crypto exchange organizations listed in its registry.
The regulator also says individuals cannot move crypto from a digital account to their own non-custodial wallet, meaning a wallet where the owner holds the private keys instead of a company. Transfers from one person to another through addresses run by a digital depository—a licensed firm that records who owns which coins—are off the table too, even to settle a trade between them.
Lending crypto is also off-limits for ordinary users: only brokers, trustees, exchange organizations, and clearing houses can act as the lender in a crypto loan.
Since Binance sold its Russian business to CommEX in 2023, a standard way for Russians to get stablecoins has been peer to peer: the buyer wires rubles to a seller’s bank card and receives USDT, a dollar-pegged token, in return. That model is exactly what the new rules end.
From July 1, 2027, Russian banks will have to refuse clients who try to fund crypto wallets on foreign platforms, and won’t be able to accept rubles cashed out from those platforms, Andrei Tugarin, managing partner at GMT Legal, told Kommersant FM.
Non-qualified investors, meaning people without professional investor status, have to pass a test and can buy up to 300,000 rubles (about $3,600) of crypto a year, while qualified investors face no cap. Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT are the only coins on the central bank’s list for non-qualified buyers.
Sberbank, Russia’s largest lender, joined the central bank’s register of crypto exchange organizations on October 12 and plans to launch its first crypto products on December 1, per Interfax. VTB and T-Invest Lab are also on that register.
Crypto exchange organizations must be Russian companies with at least 15 million rubles (about $179,000) in equity and be listed in the central bank’s registry, though they can keep operating without registration until July 1, 2027.
The law still bars Russians from spending crypto at home, keeping the ban on paying for goods and services with digital assets while allowing crypto in foreign trade settlements—a carve-out Kaplan Panesh, deputy chair of the Duma’s budget committee, openly described as a way of circumventing sanctions when the bill cleared its first reading in April.

articles.title: Ledger Unveils $849 Atom Crypto Security Device for 2027
articles.text:
Ledger’s answer to wallet tampering costs $849 and ships next year
Ledger’s new Atom combines crypto wallet security with everyday apps and is expected to ship in summer 2027 as the company investigates tampered wallets sold in Asia.
Ledger unveiled a new device on Thursday with stronger protections against tampering, days after confirming that wallets sold through a reseller in Asia contained malicious implants.
The French hardware wallet maker introduced Atom, an $849 device that combines a crypto wallet with everyday apps through a smartphone-like design. Atom separates Android apps from sensitive wallet operations and includes protections Ledger says would block the implants used in the recent Asia incident. It’s also advertised to detect tampering even when switched off.
The company expects to begin shipping the device in summer 2027, according to an announcement shared with Cointelegraph.
Ledger said Atom will also support AI agent approvals, encrypted messaging and post-quantum cryptography.
The announcement follows a security incident that surfaced on Friday involving malicious implants found in wallets sold through authorized reseller CryptoBilis. Ledger has requested that distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong suspend sales of its products. European retail chain MediaMarkt has also pulled Ledger wallets off its shelves.
Asked when Atom’s anti-tampering protections were developed, a Ledger spokesperson said the work was not a response to isolated incidents. The spokesperson did not provide a development timeline.
In a separate blog post on Thursday, Ledger said it had introduced new rules requiring authorized resellers to keep devices off display and hand them to customers at purchase. It also reiterated that returned devices must never be resold.

articles.title: Boom or Bust, Bitcoin Wins the AI Trade, Bitwise CIO Says - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan argued in an investor note that Bitcoin benefits across nearly every macro scenario, framing it like the “Choose Your Own Adventure” books where different paths reach the same ending.
- If AI delivers “superabundance,” value flows to scarce assets like Bitcoin; if the AI bubble bursts, he sees a near-certain government bailout and money-printing that Bitcoin “was built for.”
- He hedged—citing Bitcoin’s 50% COVID drop and risks like a crackdown or quantum computing, but concluded macro “matters less than most people think.”
No matter how the AI story ends, Bitwise’s chief investment officer argues, the trade leads to the same place: Bitcoin higher.
In a note to investors published Wednesday, Matt Hougan laid out his case using the “Choose Your Own Adventure” books of his childhood, where wildly different choices often funneled readers to the same ending.
He said the range of macro outcomes facing investors today is the widest he’s seen in his career, with pundits split between AI doubling GDP and AI causing human extinction. His answer was to walk down each path and see where it leads.
If AI delivers “superabundance,” Hougan wrote, productivity explodes and intelligence-based work gets cheap, but that abundance becomes a tailwind for genuinely scarce assets, as value migrates to things that can’t be reproduced, like waterfront land, gold, and Bitcoin.
If the AI bubble bursts instead, triggering a 2008-style recession, Bitcoin initially sells off with other risk assets, but Hougan argued a government bailout would follow, and given that the AI buildout is “the biggest infrastructure investment in the history of America,” the resulting money-printing would be enormous.
“This is exactly the environment bitcoin was built for,” he wrote, putting the odds of a bailout at “nearly 100%.”
The third path, a muddle-through of roughly 3% growth and 4% rates, simply lets Bitcoin keep doing what it’s been doing: drawing ETF flows, advisor adoption and corporate and sovereign balance-sheet allocations as government debt mounts. “Bitcoin wins by showing up,” he wrote.
The memo lands amid exactly the kind of macro anxiety Hougan is addressing. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned this week that a halt to data center construction could tip the U.S. into recession, underscoring how tightly AI infrastructure and the broader economy have become intertwined.
Hougan was careful to hedge. He stressed Bitcoin won’t rise in a straight line, noting it fell 50% in days during the 2020 COVID panic before rebounding roughly 20-fold, and acknowledged the thesis could break for non-macro reasons. Among them: a global government crackdown or the quantum-computing threat to older wallets, a rising risk even as researchers debate whether AI could break crypto’s encryption before quantum computers arrive.
Still, his conclusion was unequivocal: for long-term investors, the big macro questions “matter less than most people think,” because nearly every path still ends with Bitcoin.

articles.title: BlackRock’s Larry Fink Warns AI Data Center Halt Could Tip US Into Recession - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- BlackRock CEO Larry Fink says a U.S. moratorium on data center construction would trigger a recession, saying “so much of our economy is based on the build-out of this capex.”
- He dismissed the mounting backlash—over electricity, water and grid strain—as “misinformation,” insisting “data centers are not the problem."
- The warning matters for crypto given Bitcoin’s macro sensitivity.
BlackRock CEO Larry Fink has a blunt warning about what could derail the U.S. economy: slamming the brakes on the data centers powering the AI boom.
Speaking to CNBC on Wednesday after BlackRock posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, Fink said the surge in AI infrastructure spending has become so central to economic growth that choking it off would be dangerous.
“If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession,” he said, adding that “so much of our economy is based on the build-out of this capex.”
The comments come as data centers have become a flashpoint ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with local opposition mounting over their electricity demands, water use and strain on power grids.
According to Brookings, at least 100 localities had approved moratoriums by July, and New York has paused certain permits for up to a year. Fink pushed back on the backlash, calling much of it “misinformation” and insisting that “data centers are not the problem,” pointing instead to the construction jobs and energy-infrastructure demand the buildout is generating.
The scale of the spending underscores his argument. Wall Street analysts estimate AI capital expenditures could top $1 trillion in 2027 and exceed $5 trillion cumulatively through 2030, making the sector a meaningful driver of the roughly 3% annualized GDP growth Fink wants to sustain. He has argued more private capital is needed to keep it going, and said BlackRock has spoken with chipmakers including AMD and Broadcom about the effort.
But Fink is swimming against a sharply rising tide of public opposition. An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey this summer found 61% of Americans oppose new data centers in their area, up from 49% in the spring, with majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents all against them.
The concerns center on soaring electricity demand, water use and strain on local grids. That backlash has already produced real restrictions: New York has a moratorium on hyperscale data centers, Texas has paused approvals, and cities from Austin to Jersey City have imposed limits, with Data Center Watch counting roughly $130 billion in projects blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026 alone.
It has also become a live electoral issue. The fight is central to Ohio’s Senate race, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has campaigned against the buildout, and a super PAC backed by AI billionaires including Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman has poured millions into ads defending data centers across battleground states. President Donald Trump has weighed in too, warning that communities resisting the facilities risk ending up “backwards and poor.”
Against that backdrop, Fink pushed back directly, suggesting the AI buildout in the United States is propping up the U.S. economy and any shift would result in a significant downturn.
The warning carries weight for crypto, given how closely Bitcoin now tracks broader risk sentiment and macro conditions.
Fink, who runs the world’s largest asset manager and oversees its dominant spot Bitcoin ETF, has become one of Wall Street’s most prominent crypto converts. He has called Bitcoin an asset for a “frightened world” and framed it as a legitimate alternative investment, while BlackRock has flagged AI agents as a potential next wave of crypto demand.

articles.title: White House Crypto Council Director Patrick Witt Steps Down
articles.text:
White House crypto council chief Patrick Witt steps down
Witt’s departure leaves a leadership gap at the White House Crypto Council and marks the fourth high-profile exit from the advisory group.
Patrick Witt, the executive director of the White House’s Crypto Council, is leaving his current role for a new opportunity in the private sector.
“Serving in this administration has been the privilege of a lifetime,” wrote Witt in a Thursday X post, adding that he looks forward to continuing to support US technological advancements “in the private sector.”
Witt served as the White House’s leading advisor on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, would have created the first comprehensive US regulatory framework for the crypto market. The US Senate failed to pass a cloture motion on the legislation in September and further progress this session is unlikely.
Witt’s exit leaves a leadership gap as he was the last remaining staffer on the White House’s council, following the March departure of White House crypto and AI czar, David Sacks and the July departure of deputy director Harry Jung.
The council’s former executive director, Bo Hines, announced his departure in August 2025. Weeks later, Hines took a role as a strategic adviser at stablecoin issuer Tether, to coordinate the company’s US expansion.
Cointelegraph has approached the White House for comment on Witt’s departure and whether they have a potential replacement to fill his role and will update when available.
Related: Patrick Witt defers military training as CLARITY heads to Senate

articles.title: Google Says AI Isn't Building Itself Yet—Even Though It Writes 75% of the Code - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Google DeepMind found no statistically significant acceleration in the pace of its AI progress after April 1, 2026; its capability index has climbed a steady 0.1 points a month.
- Most production code at the lab is now more than 75% AI-written, but about 88% of code changes still need humans to steer the AI or write code themselves.
- Gemini 4 Argon solved roughly half of the internal research engineering tasks it finished, far below the 90% score DeepMind treats as a red flag for full automation.
Google DeepMind went looking for proof that AI is speeding up the development of AI itself. It didn’t find any.
In the safety report for Gemini 4 Argon, its most powerful model, the lab concluded AI research isn’t moving any faster, even though AI now writes most of the code DeepMind’s engineers ship.
The finding cuts against the scenario that has spooked AI executives into calling for a slowdown. It’s called recursive self-improvement: an AI builds a smarter version of itself, which builds an even smarter one, until progress outruns anyone’s ability to test, regulate, or switch it off—what the report calls “a situation where existing guardrails are severely inadequate.”
“There is currently no significant end-to-end acceleration of ML R&D, AI-driven or otherwise,” Haydn Belfield, a Google DeepMind researcher who worked on the assessment, wrote in a thread on X. “We therefore conclude that the risk from AI-driven ML R&D is currently low.”
ML R&D is shorthand for machine learning research and development, the work of building new AI models.
1/9 
In the Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, we published our first holistic empirical assessment of ML R&D automation and acceleration inside Google DeepMind — combining capability benchmarks, a macro capability index, data on AI-written code and trajectory outcomes, and… pic.twitter.com/Vr8Q5Obbsp
— Haydn Belfield (@HaydnBelfield) October 14, 2026
DeepMind tracks the issue because “AI could speed up frontier capability gains faster than safety, governance, and societal adaptation can keep pace,” Belfield wrote. More automation also means giving AI agents broader access to company systems, more room for a misaligned model (one pursuing goals its makers never intended) to cause trouble.
To measure progress, the team built GCI v1, an internal index that blends the scores of 123 AI models across 92 benchmarks into a single number per model—think of it as an IQ score for AI. “Frontier Gemini capabilities have improved at a remarkably steady pace of ~0.1 GCI points/month,” Belfield wrote.
In the report’s chart of that index, Gemini 1.5 Pro sits near 0.5 points in late 2024 and Gemini 3.8 Flash just above 2.9 in September 2026, with nearly every release hugging a straight line. Argon is the one dot poking above it, at roughly 3.3, though its error bar (the range its true score could plausibly fall in) stretches low enough to touch the trend.
“While Gemini 4 Argon sits above [the] trend, we trace this to increased compute and organizational investment rather than reflecting AI-driven acceleration,” Belfield wrote. Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on September 30.
Most production code at DeepMind is now more than 75% AI-written, and the share of fully delegated pull requests (bundles of code changes submitted for review before they go live) rose from 7.5% to 11.9% between April and September. But “~88% of pull requests still require multi-turn human steering or human code authorship—and code changes remain subject to human review before submission,” Belfield wrote.
A survey of 12 senior DeepMind leaders and researchers found automation is highest in “well-specified, verifiable execution tasks and lowest in open-ended scientific ideation, novel experimental design, diagnosing subtle training instabilities, and long-horizon research taste.” In plain terms, AI is great at executing instructions and bad at deciding which ideas are worth chasing.
DeepMind also reviewed 1,389 logs of Argon working as an agent inside the company. The bigger the task, the less likely the model finished it alone and the more often a human stepped in.
The report landed a month after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that recursive self-improvement is already accelerating, a warning Sam Altman and Elon Musk endorsed and one that sent chip stocks down almost 6%. Days earlier, former Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon had quit the industry, warning AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade.”
DeepMind’s numbers cover only its own lab, and the same report says it can’t rule out that an unrestricted Argon crosses its danger thresholds for cyberattacks and bioweapons information.

articles.title: Starknet Opens Vote on Potential Ethereum L2 Exit
articles.text:
Starknet opens vote on potential Ethereum L2 exit over quantum risks
Starknet is asking STRK holders whether to explore becoming an independent layer-1 blockchain to reduce its dependence on Ethereum’s quantum-security upgrade timeline.
Ethereum layer-2 network Starknet has opened a non-binding vote asking STRK holders whether it should explore becoming an independent, post-quantum layer-1 blockchain.
On Thursday, Starknet opened a seven-day poll, which offers three options: support further research, oppose it, or remain neutral pending more information. Voting closes on Oct. 22, with results published afterwards.
A “Yes” vote would signal support for further research, not authorize a transition. Further proposals and governance votes would be required, and no timetable for becoming an L1 has been announced.
StarkWare, the developer behind Starknet, said the move could allow the network to pursue quantum-resistant security without depending on Ethereum’s upgrade schedule. Starknet currently relies on Ethereum for infrastructure, including its bridge and data availability, which StarkWare identifies as remaining quantum-security dependencies.
“Quantum-proofing crypto is urgent, so we must move at lightning speed,” StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson told Cointelegraph, contrasting the proposal with what he described as slower progress at Ethereum and Bitcoin.
Both Ben-Sasson and Starknet hinted at the proposal in separate X posts on Oct. 8, framing it as a move to become “the first fully quantum-resistant network” by 2027.
In June, StarkWare unveiled a three-phase quantum-resistance roadmap for Starknet, covering signature upgrades, smart-contract migration and Ethereum-dependent infrastructure.
In March, Ethereum developers established a dedicated post-quantum team, aiming to introduce initial protocol-level protections by 2029.
Related: Starknet introduces wallet privacy feature for DeFi activity

articles.title: Bitget, Liquid Exploits Push Crypto Hacks near $1.2B in Q3
articles.text:
Bitget, Liquid exploits push Q3 crypto hacks toward $1.2B
Compromised suppliers, developer tools and infrastructure components outside security audits drove about 77% of the quarter’s total losses, according to Hacken.
Cryptocurrency hacks soared to $1.18 billion across 107 recorded incidents in the third quarter of 2026, according to security company Hacken.
Hacken’s Q3 report attributed 77% (about $906 million) to compromised suppliers or developer tools, publicly disclosed fixes that had not been deployed, or other components outside security reviews.
The four largest incidents included the $387 million Bitget hack, the $320 million Liquid Network exploit, the $120 million Tectonic exploit, and the Coldcard firmware vulnerability, associated with an estimated $115 million in losses.
This Q3 was the most damaging quarter for crypto hacks since Q1 2025, when Bybit’s $1.4 billion loss to North Korea pushed the total to $1.6 billion.
Q3 losses in total amount and composition. Source: Hacken
About 80% of the quarter’s losses were concentrated in four of the largest incidents, while 98 of the incidents recorded losses below $10 million. The median loss across all 107 incidents was $670,000.
While supplier compromises and infrastructure failures drove much of the stolen value, smart contract incidents were the most frequent, accounting for $228 million in losses across 71 incidents as the most exploited attack vector.
Related: Anthropic warns ‘AI worms’ may autonomously spread across devices like a virus
About a third of losses was returned or reversed after Q3 crypto hacks
Of the $1.18 billion lost, about $387 million was returned or reversed, accounting for the recovery of about 33% of gross losses.
Following the Liquid Network hack, self-proclaimed “white hats” returned $272 million, representing about 85% of the stolen value.
In the Tectonic incident, Cronos validators rolled back 114 minutes of settled blockchain history, reversing about $111.2 million of the $120.4 million in affected borrowing. Also, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether froze about $340,000 tied to the Bitget theft.
Operators covered an additional $410 million of user losses from their own funds. Bitget’s user protection fund covered $387 million, while Triple-A, Coinsbuy and TAC repaid about $22 million, making users whole, while stolen assets remained with attackers.
About $384 million, or 32% of gross losses, was neither returned nor covered.
Amount of losses covered by operators, compared to amount returned or reversed. Source: Hacken
Hacken urged industry participants to strengthen the cybersecurity of third-party suppliers, developer tools and other external infrastructure that may fall outside security audits.
The company also recommended that protocols expand security audits to include oracles, bridgers, custody systems, signing authorities and other privileged components.

articles.title: Mastercard and BVNK Launch 'Global Money Platform' to Merge Fiat and Stablecoins - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Mastercard and BVNK launched the Global Money Platform, a modular infrastructure layer letting businesses embed multi-currency accounts holding fiat and stablecoins side by side.
- It ties into Mastercard Move for local-currency payouts and lets users spend stablecoin balances across Mastercard’s merchant network, with Nuvei and Marqeta among first integrators.
- Mastercard framed it for a “multi-money” future, with planned support for agentic commerce and tokenized deposits.
Mastercard is folding stablecoins into its sprawling payments empire, launching a platform that lets businesses hold, move, and spend traditional currencies and digital dollars side by side through a single connection.
Unveiled Thursday, the Mastercard Global Money Platform pairs the payments giant’s global network with the stablecoin infrastructure of BVNK, the crypto firm Mastercard acquired in August.
Mastercard struck the deal to buy BVNK for roughly $1.8 billion, and the new platform marks the first major integration of the two companies’ capabilities since that acquisition closed.
At the center of the platform is what Mastercard calls a global money account, a multi-currency account where fiat and stablecoins can sit together, with conversion between them handled through a single API.
Banks, fintechs and enterprises can embed those accounts into their own branded products, along with real-time conversion, stablecoin-linked cards and local bank payouts, or use the platform to run their own treasury and settlement. The pitch is a modular toolkit spanning sending, receiving, converting, storing, spending and earning, letting customers start with the pieces they need and bolt on more over time.
Mastercard framed the offering as plumbing for a “multi-money” world. The platform ties into Mastercard Move, the company’s money-transfer network, letting users tap stablecoin balances to send local-currency payments into recipients’ bank accounts, with coverage expected to reach more than 40 currencies across 200-plus countries in 2027. Customers will also be able to spend stablecoin balances across Mastercard’s merchant-acceptance network, with card issuing available in more than 130 countries.
Payments firm Nuvei and card-issuing platform Marqeta are among the first to integrate the platform, alongside Ontop, Beem, and Almond FinTech.
Raj Dhamodharan, Mastercard’s executive vice president for blockchain and digital assets, said the company believes “the future of commerce will be built on interoperability across multiple forms of money,” calling the launch a step toward enabling “the next generation of programmable and agentic commerce.”
That nod to agentic commerce, where AI agents transact on their own, signals where Mastercard sees the puck heading.
The company has already moved to enable AI-agent payments alongside crypto heavyweights like Coinbase and Ripple, and secured a New York BitLicense covering stablecoins and tokenized deposits. Mastercard said Global Money Platform will add support for agentic commerce and tokenized deposits down the line.
