articles.title: AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
articles.text:
AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Indian Institute of Science (IISc)
- Summary:
- Scientists used artificial intelligence to uncover nearly 10,000 chemical reactions involved in transforming carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals, revealing crucial pathways that traditional models had missed. The discovery dramatically improved predictions of CO2 conversion and uncovered a surprising hydrogen reaction that could inspire more efficient catalysts.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered thousands of previously overlooked chemical reactions that could help improve the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) into valuable fuels and industrial chemicals. By combining machine learning with advanced computer simulations, researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) identified 9,389 individual reactions occurring on a copper catalyst, revealing unexpected chemical pathways that conventional models had missed.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help scientists develop more effective catalysts for transforming CO2 into useful products such as methanol. The research also uncovered a surprising way hydrogen can participate in these reactions, challenging established assumptions about how the process works.
One promising approach to recycling carbon dioxide is hydrogenation, which uses a catalyst to help CO2 react with hydrogen and form chemicals such as methanol. However, the process involves an enormous number of individual reactions taking place across the catalyst's surface. Simulating every possible step using quantum mechanics would require immense computing power, so researchers typically focus on a limited selection of reactions believed to be the most important. This simplification can leave hundreds of potentially critical reactions out of the picture.
"We began with a worry familiar to anyone who does mechanistic modeling: How do you know that your reaction network has not omitted the one step that matters?" says first author Anand Mohan Verma, who conducted the research as a CV Raman Postdoctoral Fellow at IISc and is now an Assistant Professor at the Motilal Nehru National Institute of Technology Allahabad (MNNIT Allahabad).
AI Reveals Thousands of Overlooked Chemical Reactions
To overcome this limitation, the research team began by using quantum mechanics simulations to build a detailed database containing 152 chemical reactions. They then trained machine learning models to quickly estimate the energy barriers that additional reactions would need to overcome.
Using automated computational tools, the scientists examined the possible reactions involving 105 chemical species present on the catalyst surface. They also determined which transformations could take place in a single reaction step. This approach expanded their original network from just 152 reactions to 9,389.
The difference was significant. When the researchers relied on the smaller network, their model incorrectly identified formic acid as the main product rather than methanol. It also predicted substantially less CO2 conversion than experiments indicated.
"When we modeled the process using the 152 reactions considered initially, the network wrongly predicted formic acid, not methanol, as the major product, and underestimated how much CO2 gets converted. Only when we expanded the network to include thousands of additional, previously overlooked reactions did the predictions fall in line with what we and others see experimentally," explains corresponding author Ananth Govind Rajan, Associate Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering, IISc.
Expanded Model Predicts 40 Times More CO2 Conversion
When the scientists incorporated the larger reaction network into a model of how quickly the chemical processes occur, the predicted amount of CO2 conversion increased by approximately 40 times compared with the original model.
The expanded model also correctly identified methanol and carbon monoxide as major products, bringing its predictions into agreement with experimental findings.
Experimental validation was carried out by G Valavarasu and Santhosh Kotni at Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited's Green Research and Development Centre, along with Amol Amrute and colleagues at the Agency for Science, Technology, and Research in Singapore. Ambedkar Dukkipati, Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Automation at IISc, also contributed to the machine learning models.
A Surprising Hydrogen Pathway Challenges Conventional Chemistry
Beyond improving the predictions, the much larger reaction network exposed an unexpected mechanism involving hydrogen.
In several important reaction steps, hydrogen could be transferred to intermediate chemical compounds directly as molecular H2, rather than only through separate hydrogen atoms. Additional quantum mechanics calculations confirmed that this pathway can be especially favorable when hydrogen is transferred to intermediates containing oxygen.
This finding challenges a long-standing assumption about how hydrogen participates in catalytic reactions and could provide valuable clues for designing better catalysts.
"The idea that hydrogen can transfer as an intact molecule, without first splitting into atoms, runs against what most of us were taught," says co-author Shivam Chaturvedi, PhD student in the Department of Chemical Engineering, IISc. "This surfaced only because the network was large enough to allow for it, and the observation held up when we went back and computed those steps explicitly. This also suggests that catalysts that interact more strongly with H2 could potentially enhance pathways leading to methanol."
The researchers believe this unexpected mechanism could guide the development of catalysts that interact more effectively with molecular hydrogen, potentially improving the chemical pathways responsible for producing methanol from CO2.
The broader computational framework may also prove useful well beyond carbon dioxide hydrogenation. By integrating quantum mechanics simulations, machine learning, automated identification of chemical reactions, and models of reaction rates, the approach could help researchers investigate other important industrial processes.
Potential applications include CO2 reduction using different catalysts, nitrogen reduction, and water splitting. By revealing chemical steps that simpler models might miss, the technique offers scientists a more complete picture of complex catalytic reactions and new opportunities to improve processes used to produce fuels and chemicals.

Journal Reference:

Data-driven massive reaction networks reveal mechanistic pathways underlying catalytic CO2 hydrogenation. Nature Communications, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77080-4

articles.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
articles.text:
DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
Scientists have recorded how a single fertilized egg becomes a complex body, uncovering hidden patterns of development that could shed light on birth defects and cancer.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Washington School of Medicine/UW Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.
- Share:
Scientists have reconstructed a remarkably detailed family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo, tracing their origins back to the moment a fertilized egg first divided into two cells. Using an innovative DNA recording technology, the researchers followed how those early cells multiplied, developed specialized roles, and eventually helped form a body with distinct organs and tissues.
The recording covered the first 13.5 days of embryonic development, providing an unusually detailed look at how a complex mammalian body takes shape. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.)
The findings, published on October 8, 2026, in the journal Science, could help scientists better understand normal development and what happens when that process goes wrong.
"We are interested in tracking how cells' early ancestry in an embryo influences their later fates. Exploring cell lineages helps decode normal development. Such research could eventually advance knowledge about congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental conditions, genetic disorders or cancer," said Dr. Jay Shendure, a professor of genome sciences at the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator.
Shendure led the research alongside Dr. Chengxiang Qiu, a molecular and systems biologist at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Both served as senior authors of the study.
A DNA Typewriter Records the History of Living Cells
The achievement was made possible by a technology called DNA Typewriter, developed by Shendure and Junhong Choi, who is now at Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
Rather than simply observing cells as they divide, the system allows scientists to preserve a record of their history directly within their DNA.
To accomplish this, the researchers inserted a redesigned recording sequence, which they call a tape, into the genome of a fertilized mouse egg. The updated design made it easier to recover the information stored in individual cells.
As the embryo developed, the DNA Typewriter remained embedded in the genetic material of its cells, recording their divisions in a way that could later be used to reconstruct their ancestry. The result was something like a biological logbook, documenting the sequence of events that gave rise to different cell populations.
"Think of it like an actual typewriter, except it types onto a cell's own DNA instead of paper," explained Haedong Kim, a co-first author of the study and a postdoctoral scientist in genome sciences at UW Medicine, the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. "Every time a cell divides, it strikes one new character onto the next blank line -- always in order, never overwriting what's already there. Because the characters are always filled in sequence, that sequence itself spells out the cell's division history."
Because these markings are passed down to daughter cells, researchers can examine the recorded sequences and identify which cells descended from a shared ancestor. Cells carrying matching portions of the record can be linked together, allowing scientists to reconstruct branches of the embryo's family tree.
"Writing the record is only half the problem. You also have to read it back out of each cell, so we redesigned the tape to make that easier," said Kim.
Overcoming a Major Challenge in Developmental Biology
Reconstructing the entire history of a developing mammal has long been a formidable challenge. As an embryo grows, its cells divide repeatedly and begin taking on specialized functions. Following those relationships becomes increasingly difficult as the number and variety of cells expand.
Scientists accomplished a similar feat decades ago in a tiny roundworm, but that animal has a relatively simple body with far fewer cells. Its transparency also makes development easier to study.
Mammals are considerably more complicated. Earlier technologies provided important insights into mouse embryonic development, but they generally captured only portions of the larger cellular family tree.
Some traditional recording techniques also have significant limitations. They work by cutting DNA to create identifying marks, which can damage cells and erase information left by earlier divisions. Their recording capacity is limited, and because the marks are not necessarily created in a fixed sequence, scientists must attempt to reconstruct the order of events afterward.
"DNA Typewriter avoids all of this," said Kim. "It writes without fully severing the DNA, keeps recording relatively steadily, and writes everything in strict order, so we can record cell lineages at much higher resolution for a longer time."
Tracing an Embryo Back to Its First Two Cells
The researchers began by attempting to record development in 100 fertilized mouse eggs. Of those, 10 embryos were ultimately available for examination.
One specimen, identified as Embryo No. 3, stood out because its DNA recording system had functioned particularly well and preserved the most extensive developmental history. The scientists therefore concentrated their detailed analysis on that embryo.
One of the most important discoveries came from a recording made at the very beginning of development, immediately after the fertilized egg divided for the first time.
"Our recording captured a clear, permanent mark distinguishing the two very first cells, letting us trace nearly every cell we profiled from the embryo back to one or the other," said Kim. "One of these two founding cells did go on to produce more descendants than the other, but they produced diverse cell types at almost equal ratios."
This meant that although one of the original cells contributed more descendants overall, both founding cells gave rise to a remarkably similar mix of specialized cell types.
The finding illustrates how scientists can now investigate the earliest stages of development with a level of detail that was previously difficult to achieve.
Scientists Discover When Cells Choose Their Roles
The DNA recordings also revealed important information about when cells begin committing to their eventual roles in the body.
Early embryonic cells can give rise to many different types of tissue. As development progresses, their descendants gradually become more specialized, eventually forming structures such as the nervous system, skin, blood, and eyes.
By reconstructing the branches of the embryo's cellular family tree, the researchers could determine when different groups of cells began following distinct developmental paths.
Their observations were consistent with conclusions drawn from decades of previous research, but the new approach allowed them to examine these patterns within a single developing mouse.
"Blood cells and the retina committed relatively early, while the skin's outer layer didn't commit until noticeably later," the researchers explained. "Cell fate wasn't locked in all at once. Different cell types settled into their identity on their own separate schedules, some early and some late."
These findings show that the transition from a flexible, unspecialized cell to one with a particular biological function does not happen at the same time throughout the embryo.
Instead, different tissues follow their own developmental timelines. Some cells begin narrowing their possible futures early, while others remain flexible for a longer period before becoming committed to a specific role.
What This Could Mean for Birth Defects, Cancer, and Stem Cell Therapies
Understanding exactly how cells acquire their identities could eventually have important implications for medicine.
Many developmental disorders arise when the normal process of cell specialization or tissue formation is disrupted. Cancer also involves abnormal cell behavior, including failures in the mechanisms that ordinarily regulate cell growth and division.
By tracing cellular ancestry and identifying when different developmental pathways emerge, scientists may gain a clearer understanding of how these problems begin.
"This kind of large-scale developmental recording gives scientists a map of how one cell becomes a whole body -- which helps explain how organs form correctly, how that process can go wrong in birth defects, and how abnormal cell growth drives cancer. As stem cell engineering advances, this kind of recording can also help guide how we engineer cells for therapeutic use."
Although the work was conducted in mouse embryos and does not yet represent a direct medical treatment, it demonstrates a powerful way to study the biological decisions that shape a developing organism.
The approach could also support future stem cell research, particularly efforts to guide cells toward specific identities for regenerative medicine and other therapeutic applications.
Research Team and Funding
Additional co-first authors included Qi Yu and Sophie Seidel, both affiliated with the University of Washington School of Medicine's Department of Genome Sciences and the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology.
Shendure serves as the lead scientific director of the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology. He is also scientific director of the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine and the Allen Institute for Cell Lineage Tracing.
The research received support from the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology, a collaboration involving the Allen Institute, BioHub, and University of Washington School of Medicine (CZIF2023-008738); the Paul G. Allen Frontiers Group's Allen Discovery Center for Cell Lineage Tracing; the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine; the Washington Research Foundation; the National Institutes of Health (R00HG012973 and P30CA008748); the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation (DFS-64-24); the Searle Scholars Award (SSP-2025-101); Dartmouth's Center for Quantitative Biology through a National Institute of General Medical Sciences grant (P20GM130454); and the Swiss National Science Foundation (239394).

A DNA Typewriter records the cell lineage history of a mouse, from zygote to late organogenesis. Science, 2026; DOI: 10.1126/science.ael0508

articles.title: 210-million-year-old dinosaur discovery reveals a lost world in Africa
articles.text:
210-million-year-old dinosaur discovery reveals a lost world in Africa
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A newly identified 210-million-year-old dinosaur from Zimbabwe is helping scientists uncover a surprisingly distinct prehistoric ecosystem. The discovery suggests that ancient climate differences may have separated dinosaur populations across southern Africa, leading to unique species that challenge previous assumptions about their evolution.
- Share:
Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth’s animal and plant species. This diversity is driven by diverse habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries.
Africa is most famous for spectacular hominid fossils that reveal our own ancestry. However, the continent boasts many fabulous fossil finds, including those of the most familiar extinct animals – dinosaurs.
The first African dinosaur fossils to be noted scientifically hailed from the Eastern Cape, South Africa and were described in the 1850s. Since then, the African dinosaur map has expanded, with rich fossil beds in South Africa, Lesotho, Tanzania, Egypt, Niger, Malawi, Madagascar and Morocco.
Zimbabwe is an important part of the African dinosaur puzzle, with dinosaur bones reported since 1916.
As a specialist on early dinosaurs who has worked on similar material from China, the UK and Africa, I’ve been drawn to these Zimbabwean fossils to see what they reveal about the first stages of their evolution.
Our latest addition to the Triassic zoo, Musango matusadonaensis, is a sauropodomorph dinosaur. (That’s the dinosaur subgroup that eventually gave rise to four-legged, long-necked giants like Diplodocus.)
Its incomplete skeleton was found in the bank of the Nyamasango River close to Musango Island, as captured in the animal’s scientific name. Musango’s anatomy shows us that it was bipedal (walking on its hind legs only), reached about 4.5 meters in length, and weighed 220kg. Growth marks in its bones reveal that it was a subadult when it died. Sadly, the skull wasn’t preserved, so its diet is unknown, but its close relatives were largely herbivorous (plant-eating).
Our new work reveals something unexpected about Zimbabwean dinosaurs. They’re not simply an extension of better-known South African faunas but include an array of species unique to the region. We’re now trying to work out why these differences exist. We suspect that environmental conditions might be the key.
The search
Early fossil finds in Zimbabwe were overlooked by many scientists and it was not until the 1970s that they became more generally known. This was thanks to pioneering work by Zimbabwean paleontologists Geoffrey Bond and Michael Raath, who discovered abundant material in the hinterlands of Bulawayo (south-west Zimbabwe) and the lower Zambezi Valley (forming the border with Zambia). Most of these finds were identified as belonging to known species named from neighboring South Africa.
Paleontological work in Zimbabwe stalled for a few decades. However, a band of devoted fossil hunters kept searching. One of them, Steve Edwards, a local safari camp manager, found new, productive sites on the shore of Lake Kariba, the artificial lake which forms most of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. News of the discoveries eventually reached Jonah Choiniere at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg. Jonah, an expert on early dinosaurs, immediately recognized the importance of the material. He assembled an international team of South African, Zimbabwean and UK-based collaborators to explore them further.
This was a major task, as the sites on Late Kariba’s shoreline are deep inside Matusadona National Park. Our solution was to use one of the Kariba houseboats as a mobile hotel and laboratory, so that we could prospect the shoreline. We mounted two expeditions, in 2017 and 2018. We have been cleaning and studying this material ever since.
Both trips yielded a trove of material, collected from brick-red mudstones and sandstones that were laid down by ancient rivers around 210 million years ago, during the Late Triassic period (237-201 million years ago). Geological evidence and plant fossils show that the Triassic landscape of Kariba was dry and dotted with stands of large conifer trees, with green corridors of vegetation following permanent watercourses.
What’s unique
Sauropodomorphs are the most common Late Triassic dinosaurs. But what’s interesting about Musango and its relative Musankwa (which we described from the same beds in 2024) is that they are unique to Zimbabwe.
We’d expected to find South African dinosaur species in these beds, given their similar age and geographic proximity, but surprisingly all the material we’ve collected so far has revealed animals that are distinct from those elsewhere.
These Zimbabwean dinosaurs are not even the closest relatives of their South African neighbors. We’ve also found other fossil animals, including lungfish and aquatic reptiles called phytosaurs, which are rare or absent in South African sites.
Following this, we’ve started to reappraise the historical dinosaur collections in Bulawayo. It appears that many of these fossils can’t be referred to South African species either, contrary to earlier assumptions.
Then, as now, Zimbabwe was further north than South Africa and closer to the equator, so climatic differences might be responsible for these varied casts of characters (as climate is known to have a strong effect on the distributions of living animals). To probe this further, we’ll be going back to Kariba in search of more fossils.
We’ll also collect more information on the exact ages and environments of these dinosaur-bearing rocks, to compare them more precisely with sites elsewhere. Although the significance of these dinosaurs is only just coming to light, Zimbabwe is already taking a greater role in shedding much needed light on early dinosaur evolution.

articles.title: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.text:
James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
Webb has revealed a massive, dark matter-packed galaxy cluster that formed surprisingly early, challenging scientists’ understanding of how the universe evolved.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Caltech IPAC
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.
- Share:
A massive galaxy cluster dating back to an era when such enormous structures were only beginning to take shape is challenging scientists' understanding of how the universe evolved. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) reveal that the cluster contains an unusually dense concentration of matter, suggesting that some cosmic structures may have developed much faster than current models predict.
The galaxy cluster, known as XLSSC 122, has become the focus of three recent studies led by researchers at IPAC, Caltech's science and data center for astrophysics and planetary science. Their findings establish XLSSC 122 as the most distant galaxy cluster known to exhibit strong gravitational lensing, a phenomenon that allows astronomers to measure the mass of otherwise invisible matter. The research was presented at a press conference on June 17, 2026, during the 248th meeting of the American Astronomical Society.
Located approximately 10.4 billion light-years from Earth, XLSSC 122 stood out to astronomers because of its surprising maturity. Although it existed during a period when galaxy clusters were still assembling, it already displayed the size and organized structure typically associated with clusters in the modern universe.
Webb has now uncovered another remarkable feature. XLSSC 122 happens to lie directly in front of one or more galaxies that are even farther away. The cluster's powerful gravity bends and distorts the light traveling from those background galaxies, creating a rare effect called strong gravitational lensing. This fortunate alignment has given scientists an exceptionally precise way to measure how mass is distributed throughout the cluster.
"When we got those first images back from JWST, we said, 'wow, look at this, there's strong lensing coming from this cluster!'" said Kyle Finner, a staff scientist at IPAC and lead author of the first paper examining the cluster. "XLSSC 122 has now set the record for the most distant galaxy cluster displaying strong lensing, which is a valuable tool for astronomers."
An Ancient Galaxy Cluster Challenges Cosmic Predictions
The newly detected gravitational lensing has allowed researchers to examine the distribution of mass in an ancient galaxy cluster in greater detail than ever before. XLSSC 122 dates to a period known as "cosmic noon," roughly 10 billion years ago, when the universe was experiencing its most intense era of star formation.
During this time, galaxies were producing stars at rates up to 100 times higher than those observed in the present-day universe. Galaxy clusters were also becoming increasingly common as smaller systems gradually combined into larger structures.
Yet XLSSC 122 appears to have developed in an unexpected way. The new measurements show that a remarkably large amount of its mass is packed into its central region. According to standard cosmological models, the growth of massive structures should have been more gradual, making such a concentrated cluster particularly surprising at this early stage of cosmic history.
"XLSSC 122 is one of the first clusters we know of that formed in the universe, and it has a mass concentration that doesn't agree with our cosmological model predictions," said Finner.
To investigate the mystery further, Finner and his collaborators conducted two additional JWST studies, first authored by Zachary Scofield and Hyungjin Joo at Yonsei University. Together, the three papers provide a much more complete picture of this unusual cluster and offer new insights into galaxy cluster formation during cosmic noon.
James Webb Reveals Hidden Dark Matter
Astronomers originally identified XLSSC 122 in 2014 through an X-ray survey carried out by the European Space Agency's XMM-Newton spacecraft. Later observations with the Hubble Space Telescope helped establish its distance of approximately 10.4 billion light-years and confirmed that the cluster appeared unusually developed for its age.
However, Hubble did not reveal clear evidence of strong gravitational lensing. That changed when JWST captured distinctive curved arcs of light surrounding the cluster's center, providing the first definitive signs of this phenomenon in XLSSC 122.
"Before JWST, we couldn't do this level of science in the early, distant universe," said Finner.
The gravitational distortions are caused primarily by something astronomers cannot directly observe: dark matter.
Although XLSSC 122 contains visible stars and glowing gas, these familiar forms of matter account for only a small fraction of the gravitational lensing effect. Most of the distortion comes from dark matter, an invisible substance that has not been directly detected through light but whose gravitational influence is supported by extensive astronomical evidence.
Scientists estimate that dark matter is approximately five times more abundant than ordinary matter, which makes up stars, planets, and everything around us. Its gravity helps hold galaxies together and shapes the universe's enormous network of galaxy groups, clusters, and filaments.
Because dark matter plays such an important role in cosmic structure, determining how it was distributed billions of years ago offers a powerful way to test theories describing the universe's development since the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
"Strong lensing is a way to measure the dark matter without actually seeing the dark matter," said Finner. "It gives us a sensitive probe of our cosmological models."
A Wider View Reveals a Galaxy Cluster Merger
In their second paper, the researchers investigated XLSSC 122 using another form of gravitational lensing known as weak lensing.
Strong gravitational lensing produces obvious distortions, including the striking arcs captured by JWST. Weak lensing, by comparison, causes much smaller changes in the apparent shapes of distant galaxies. These subtle effects are difficult to identify individually, so astronomers rely on statistical methods to detect them.
The two techniques provide complementary information. Strong lensing is especially useful for measuring the mass concentrated near a cluster's center, while weak lensing can reveal how matter is distributed across its outer regions.
"Weak gravitational lensing can constrain mass much further out, so you can get a better picture of the surrounding cluster area," said Finner.
By combining these measurements with X-ray and radio observations from other telescopes, the scientists determined that XLSSC 122 is still undergoing a merger. Its galaxies are continuing to come together as the larger cluster takes shape.
The broader analysis also reinforced the earlier finding that an unusually large amount of mass is concentrated near the cluster's center.
Ancient Starlight Offers New Clues to Dark Matter
The team's third and most recent paper revealed another important feature of XLSSC 122: faint light produced by stars that are no longer bound to individual galaxies.
Known as intracluster light, this diffuse glow comes from stars scattered into the spaces between galaxies. Webb's observations represent the earliest known detection of intracluster light, providing another way to examine the development of galaxy clusters in the distant universe.
The widespread distribution of this light supports the conclusion that XLSSC 122 is undergoing a merger. As galaxies interact and collide, some stars are pulled away from their original galaxies and spread throughout the cluster. In XLSSC 122, many of these displaced stars appear not to have settled into its dense central region.
The researchers also uncovered an intriguing connection between these wandering stars and dark matter.
Near the cluster's center, the shape of the intracluster light closely matches the distribution of dark matter inferred from strong gravitational lensing. This suggests that the faint glow of stars between galaxies could potentially serve as a visible indicator of where invisible dark matter is concentrated.
If astronomers observe the same relationship in other clusters, particularly those from the early universe, intracluster light could become a valuable new tool for mapping dark matter across cosmic history.
"In this cluster, the intracluster light essentially traces the dark matter," said Finner. "That light tells us that the cluster is in a merging state."
Could More Ancient Galaxy Clusters Challenge Cosmology?
The next goal for Finner and his colleagues is to identify and investigate dozens of additional galaxy clusters from similarly early periods in the universe's history.
Finding these distant objects requires a different approach from studying them in detail. Although JWST is exceptionally powerful, its relatively narrow field of view makes it better suited to examining selected targets than searching enormous areas of the sky.
Instead, astronomers must first identify promising candidates through wide-area X-ray and radio surveys, similar to the observations that originally revealed XLSSC 122.
One promising technique relies on the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, which occurs when energetic particles inside galaxy clusters scatter radiation from the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.
This interaction can create distinctive regions that appear as "holes" in observations of the cosmic microwave background. By searching for these signatures, astronomers can locate galaxy clusters that might otherwise be difficult to detect.
Finding more objects like XLSSC 122 could have major implications for cosmology. If other ancient clusters also contain unexpectedly concentrated dark matter and display unusually advanced development, scientists may need to revise some of their basic assumptions about how quickly large cosmic structures formed.
For now, XLSSC 122 provides an important test of existing models, but a larger sample will be necessary to determine whether its unusual properties are rare or part of a broader pattern in the early universe.
"It's still early in the JWST era," said Finner, "and if we can start to get data on tens or hundreds of these types of objects at this stage in the universe, then we can really start putting our cosmological models to the test."

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising paradox in how our cells age
articles.text:
Scientists discover a surprising paradox in how our cells age
Research reveals a surprising twist in cellular aging and finds that gentle exercise may help restore a more youthful balance.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Sanford Burnham Prebys
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that the body's cellular recycling system behaves very differently during aging than previously believed, with higher activity sometimes linked to worse physical health. A small study suggests that even gentle exercise could help restore more youthful cellular recycling patterns in older adults.
- Share:
Cells rely on a natural cleanup system to prevent damaged materials from accumulating inside them. Known as autophagy, this process collects defective proteins and other cellular waste, packages them into specialized compartments, and breaks them down into basic molecular components that can be reused.
This recycling system helps protect cells from damage. Scientists have long considered declining autophagy a hallmark of aging, and problems with the process have been linked to numerous diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders.
However, new research suggests that cellular recycling does not necessarily slow down as people get older. Instead, its activity can increase, decrease, or remain unchanged depending on the type of cell and a person's sex. The findings also suggest that exercise may influence how this process functions in older adults.
Researchers at Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute reported these findings on September 27, 2026, in the journal Aging Cell, challenging a widely accepted view of how cellular recycling changes throughout life.
"We commonly see people cite this idea that autophagy declines with age, but the actual evidence for this in humans is very thin," said senior and corresponding author Caroline Kumsta, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.
"Interest is growing in targeting autophagy to develop new healthy aging interventions," said Tatiana Moreno, PhD '26, lead author of the study and a former graduate student in the Kumsta lab.
"We wanted to challenge assumptions and investigate what actually happens to autophagy during aging in healthy individuals."
How Scientists Studied Cellular Recycling and Aging
To better understand the relationship between aging and autophagy, the researchers collected blood and skin samples from volunteers between the ages of 23 and 72. All participants reported having no chronic medical conditions.
The team also converted some of the collected skin cells into induced neurons, allowing the researchers to examine cellular recycling in three different cell types.
For each cell type, the scientists analyzed RNA transcripts, which are produced when cells read genetic instructions from DNA to make proteins, enzymes, and other essential components. This analysis allowed them to examine how age and cell type affected the activity of genes involved in autophagy.
Importantly, the researchers did not rely on gene activity alone. They also directly measured how quickly cells carried out autophagy, allowing them to determine whether patterns in gene expression accurately reflected the amount of recycling taking place.
The results revealed a much more complicated picture than the traditional understanding of cellular aging.
"We found that autophagic activity changes were not universal throughout the body and did not follow the idea that autophagy simply declines with age," said Kumsta. "Rather, cellular recycling rates are altered differently with age in each of the cell types, and differently by sex in each of the cell types."
Aging Affects Different Cells in Surprising Ways
The researchers observed striking differences in how autophagy changed with age. In skin cells from male participants, recycling activity decreased as age increased. In female skin cells, it remained relatively stable. Meanwhile, induced neurons derived from female participants showed an increase in autophagy with age.
These findings demonstrate that cellular recycling does not follow a single pattern throughout the body. Instead, aging appears to affect the process differently depending on the cells being examined and the sex of the individual.
The researchers also discovered that the expression of genes responsible for autophagy did not reliably indicate how much recycling was actually occurring. Cells with higher or lower levels of autophagy gene expression did not necessarily show corresponding differences in their measured recycling rates.
"This shows that people using static measures such as transcription levels to infer what's happening with autophagy need to be really careful about their interpretations," said Moreno.
Why More Cellular Cleanup May Not Be Better
The team next investigated whether differences in autophagy were associated with physical health and performance as people age.
Their findings pointed to another unexpected possibility: higher levels of cellular recycling may have different implications for younger and older adults.
Among participants aged 70 and older, greater autophagy activity was associated with poorer measures of physical function across all three cell types studied.
In blood cells, higher autophagy was linked to lower aerobic fitness. In skin cells, it was associated with a higher body mass index (BMI). In induced neurons, increased recycling activity was connected to weaker grip strength, lower metabolism, and a higher resting heart rate.
These associations suggest that increased autophagy is not necessarily a sign of healthier aging. Although cellular recycling plays an essential protective role, its relationship with physical health may change later in life.
"I think this is an important distinction that merits continued study, as it appears that increased autophagy flux may be good in younger people yet problematic in older people," said Kumsta.
"Autophagy and aging are so much more nuanced than previously assumed," said Moreno. "To better translate autophagy research discoveries into potential therapies, we really need to understand what is happening on a cell-specific level and how it is affected by sex and age."
Gentle Exercise May Help Restore Youthful Cellular Activity
The researchers also explored whether physical activity could influence autophagy in older adults.
In a small pilot study, five participants between the ages of 77 and 88 completed a gentle exercise program lasting 12 weeks. The activities focused on reducing the risk of falls, and researchers collected blood samples both before and after the program to measure changes in cellular recycling.
The preliminary results suggested that exercise could lower autophagy activity in blood cells toward levels more typical of younger adults. Participants also showed improvements in physical performance.
Although the pilot involved only five people, the findings raise the possibility that exercise could help regulate cellular recycling in ways that support healthier aging. Larger studies will be needed to establish whether these changes are consistent and how they relate to improvements in physical health.
"It is exciting to have this exercise intervention that may have a positive effect on autophagy and healthy aging, and I'm really excited to see where that goes," said Kumsta.
Expanding Research Into Exercise and Healthy Aging
The findings highlight the importance of understanding cellular recycling as a process that changes in complex ways throughout life, rather than one that uniformly declines with age. They also suggest that future treatments targeting autophagy may need to account for a person's age, sex, and the specific cells involved.
To investigate the potential benefits of exercise further, the Kumsta laboratory received a pilot grant from the Altman Clinical and Translational Research Institute at the University of California San Diego (UC San Diego).
The team is now working with the Exercise and Physical Activity Resource Center at UC San Diego on larger studies involving more participants and improved testing methods. These efforts will examine how physical activity affects autophagy, aging, and physical function, with the goal of better understanding whether changes in cellular recycling could eventually contribute to strategies for healthier aging.

articles.title: This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
articles.text:
This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
A tiny, 165-million-year-old Jurassic predator reveals an evolutionary breakthrough that helped pave the way for modern mammals and the human brain.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bonn
- Summary:
- A 165-million-year-old fossil has revealed an extraordinary Jurassic predator that may help explain how mammals developed one of their most important evolutionary advantages. Although only 20 inches long, Megacauda sungei was a heavyweight among early mammal relatives, swimming through ancient waterways and hunting prey with specialized teeth. Its advanced swallowing anatomy reveals an early step toward the ability to safely nurse on milk, a key development in mammalian evolution.
- Share:
A furry predator that lived 165 million years ago is offering scientists an unexpected glimpse into the evolution of mammals. Known as Megacauda sungei, this ancient hunter measured only about half a meter (20 inches) from nose to tail, yet it was remarkably large compared with most of its Jurassic relatives. It hunted in the water, using teeth with backward-curving cusps to grip slippery prey.
Its most significant feature, however, was not its size or hunting ability. Researchers discovered evidence of a sophisticated soft palate that separated the mouth from the pharynx, the passage connecting the mouth to the throat. This anatomical development helped make it possible to swallow while maintaining the ability to breathe, an essential adaptation for mammals that nurse their young. The findings, from researchers in Shenyang, Chicago, and Bonn, have been published in the journal Nature.
How an Ancient Predator Reveals the Evolution of Swallowing
Many animals lack a soft palate and instead rely on a relatively simple arrangement of hyoid bones in the throat. Without the complex swallowing mechanism found in mammals, feeding can require very different movements.
Crocodiles, for example, lift their heads and make sudden jerking motions to move unchewed food down their throats. "This is achieved with the aid of gravity," explains paleontologist Prof. Dr. Thomas Martin from the University of Bonn.
Mammals have a more elaborate hyoid structure that allows them to swallow even when gravity is working against them. Humans, for instance, can drink through a straw while upside down and still breathe.
This ability has played an important role in mammalian evolution. It allows young mammals to consume nutrient-rich milk safely, preventing liquid from entering the nasal passages. By supporting effective nursing, this adaptation provided an important survival advantage.
"It was this adaptation that made brain development, eventually leading to humans, possible," stresses Martin. "The soft palate and the shaping of the oral cavity and pharynx are directly linked to the evolution of mammals."
Remarkably, Megacauda sungei already possessed evidence of this anatomical development millions of years before modern mammals appeared.
A 165-Million-Year-Old Predator Built for Swimming
With its short fur and broad, flattened tail, Megacauda sungei would have looked somewhat like a modern otter, beaver, or platypus. Its body was also well suited to moving through water.
Scientists used computed tomography scans of the fossil to create detailed three-dimensional reconstructions of its anatomy. These models suggest that the animal propelled itself through the water by paddling with its front legs and moving its tail in an undulating motion. Its hind legs likely helped it change direction.
"It is the earliest evidence of an aquatic lifestyle in mammals," says the paleontologist from the University of Bonn.
Its teeth revealed another unusual adaptation. Along with the backward-curving cusps that helped it catch aquatic prey, the animal possessed specialized canine teeth with three roots, a distinctive feature that surprised the researchers.
By comparing the fossil with other prehistoric specimens and living animals, the team determined that Megacauda sungei belonged to the docodonts, an extinct group of early mammal relatives known as mammaliaforms. These animals were especially widespread during the Jurassic Period. The fossil itself was discovered in Xiayingzi, Inner Mongolia.
A Tiny Giant in the Age of Dinosaurs
"The new species Megacauda sungei is the largest of the mammaliaforms from the Jurassic," says Thomas Martin.
At roughly half a meter long and weighing about two kilograms (4.4 pounds), this prehistoric "top predator" would seem insignificant beside modern giants such as elephants, rhinoceroses, and whales.
But size was relative in the Jurassic world.
The Mesozoic Era, which lasted from approximately 230 million to 66 million years ago, was dominated by dinosaurs. Early mammal relatives generally remained small, with many weighing only a few grams.
Against that backdrop, Megacauda sungei was unusually large. Although tiny by today's standards, this aquatic hunter was a heavyweight among the early mammal relatives that shared the planet with dinosaurs.
An Extraordinary Fossil Discovery in Inner Mongolia
The scientific importance of Megacauda sungei might never have been recognized without a fortunate series of events.
Years ago, the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning in Shenyang (China) acquired the fossil, which had been unearthed in Inner Mongolia, as part of a collection of specimens. Its exceptional features became apparent when three scientists examined it together: Prof. Dr. Chang-Fu Zhou from Shandong University (China), Prof. Dr. Zhe-Xi Luo from the University of Chicago (USA), and Prof. Dr. Thomas Martin from the University of Bonn.
Recognizing that the specimen represented a previously unknown species, the researchers chose to honor Prof. Sun Ge, the Honorary Director of the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning.
They combined the name "large tail" (Megacauda) with the species designation "sungei," creating the scientific name Megacauda sungei.
Establishing the animal's identity required years of detailed analysis, comparisons, classification, and documentation.
"It is the result of a long period of teamwork," says Thomas Martin.
The research has provided important new insights into the early history of mammals, particularly how rapidly their ancestors developed specialized bodies and lifestyles.
Other Jurassic docodont fossils show that members of this group were already adapting to very different environments. Some lived in trees, others burrowed underground like moles, and species such as Megacauda sungei were adapted to life in water.
"This shows how widespread docodonts were in the Northern Hemisphere and that this diverse group of animals developed very different lifestyles at an incredibly early stage," summarizes Martin.
Together, these discoveries reveal that long before modern mammals became dominant, their ancient relatives were already experimenting with an impressive range of ways to survive.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
articles.text:
The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
Eating breakfast, exercising, and sleeping well could help build a more flexible, resilient mind that handles stress better.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Binghamton University
- Summary:
- Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.
- Share:
Feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong? Everyday habits such as eating a nutritious breakfast, getting regular exercise, and sleeping enough may play an important role in how well your mind handles difficult situations.
New research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.
Psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change. Rather than becoming trapped in negative thinking or overwhelmed by frustration, people with greater psychological flexibility can recognize their emotions, consider their options, and respond in a more productive way.
"You might know someone who stays cool under pressure," said Lina Begdache, an associate professor of health and wellness studies at Binghamton University and lead author of the research. "The kind of person who misses a flight and, instead of panicking, calmly adapts to the situation. This person may still feel stressed, but they're better able to manage it through psychological flexibility."
"People may say that these are resilient people, but they also have what's called psychological flexibility. They're able to change the way they think about the situation and then use brain resources to handle the stress."
How Breakfast, Sleep, and Exercise Relate to Mental Resilience
To explore the relationship between lifestyle choices and emotional resilience, Begdache worked with Jason Cherry, a former Binghamton assistant professor of physical therapy, and former student Alexander J. Talkachov.
The researchers collected anonymous survey responses from approximately 400 college students, gathering information about their diets, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle factors.
Their findings revealed an important connection between healthy routines and the ability to cope with stress. Students who reported healthier habits, including regular physical activity and consistent breakfast consumption, also tended to demonstrate greater psychological flexibility and resilience.
The study identified several notable associations:
- Regular breakfast consumption: Eating breakfast at least five times per week was associated with greater resilience, with psychological flexibility helping explain the relationship.
- Adequate sleep: Students who slept fewer than six hours generally reported lower levels of both resilience and psychological flexibility.
- Physical activity: Exercise lasting 20 minutes or longer was associated with greater psychological flexibility and an improved ability to cope with stress.
- Fish oil intake: Taking fish oil several times per week was linked to better psychological flexibility.
The opposite pattern also emerged. Students who reported less healthy behaviors, including frequent fast food consumption and insufficient sleep, tended to show greater psychological rigidity, meaning they had more difficulty adjusting their thoughts and behaviors when circumstances changed.
Because the research relied on survey responses, the results demonstrate associations rather than proving that these habits directly improve psychological flexibility or resilience.
Why Psychological Flexibility Matters for Stress
According to Begdache, psychological flexibility gives people the mental space to recognize what they are experiencing instead of becoming completely absorbed by their stress. This ability to reassess a situation can make it easier to understand difficult emotions and determine how to respond.
She explained that improvements in diet and lifestyle may help support this kind of mental adaptability.
"When we're under stress, we feel like we fuse with the stress. We live the stress. But psychological flexibility is like stepping back and thinking, 'I feel this because of that. What can I do?' Identifying your emotions sometimes helps you find the solution for these emotions," said Begdache.
The findings also build on Begdache's previous research, which linked nutritious diets to greater resilience and poorer dietary habits to reduced resilience.
The latest study offers a possible explanation for that relationship. Rather than influencing resilience alone, diet and lifestyle may support psychological flexibility, which in turn helps people manage stress more effectively.
"The new finding here is that diet and lifestyle don't just make you resilient by themselves. They help you build the psychological flexibility, which, in turn, makes you a resilient person."
The study, "Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator," was published in the Journal of American College Health.

Journal Reference:
- Lina Begdache, Jason Cherry, Alexander J. Talkachov. Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator. Journal of American College Health, 2025; 74 (6): 1569 DOI: 10.1080/07448481.2025.2597907

articles.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
articles.text:
Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.
- Share:
Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.
Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.
"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease."
Researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.
Their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.
The findings were published in Nature.
Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain
To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.
The team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.
The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.
Many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.
"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," says D'Angelo.
Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps
The new atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.
One striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.
"This shows that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.
The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.
Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal important features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.
Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids
Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered new insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.
When researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.
The cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, showed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an important component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.
These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.
"Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," says Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs."
A New Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease
The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.
By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.
The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.
Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.
"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

Journal Reference:
