articles.title: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Thursday said that if Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton loses, it will be the fault of incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn and conservative commentator Karl Rove.
Trump accused Cornyn and Rove of "doing everything possible to make it hard" for Paxton, the state's attorney general, to beat Democratic nominee James Talarico. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed.
"If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump's preemptive blame-casting came as Texas has surprisingly become one of the most competitive battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm cycle. Most recent polls show state Rep. Talarico maintaining a lead in the low-to-mid single digits over Paxton.
The reliably red state has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. In 2024, Texans voted for Trump over Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by nearly 14 percentage points.
Cornyn's office and Rove did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Trump's post.
Trump's decision to back Paxton in the GOP primary delivered a major blow to the four-term incumbent Cornyn, whom the president viewed as disloyal. The move was also seen as a major gamble, as Paxton's history of scandal and opposition within his own party has made him a polarizing figure.
Hoping to stave off Democrats' goal of winning majority control of the Senate, groups backing Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Texas contest, making it the most expensive race of the cycle.
GOP spending in the race has topped $370 million so far, eclipsing Democratic spending by nearly $235 million, according to AdImpact.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Rove, calling him a "loser" and urging Fox News to stop putting him on air.
Rove, who was a senior advisor to former President George W. Bush, "is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often," Trump wrote in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post.
In a Wall Street Journal op-ed two days later, Rove said that he would back a Democratic candidate in a different race in Texas, voting blue for just the second time in his life.

articles.title: Anthropic taps nonprofits METR and SecureBio to help assess risks and safety practices
articles.text:
Anthropic on Thursday announced it's working with the nonprofits METR and SecureBio, and engaging in discussions with additional organizations, including Hugging Face, as part of its commitment to embed independent evaluators within the company.
The artificial intelligence lab pledged to work closely with third-party evaluators when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published his proposal to slow down the pace of model development last month. Amodei said the evaluators would help "verify" Anthropic's adherence to safety practices, and the company selected Accenture to serve as its first partner days later.
Independent evaluators like METR, which stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research, occupied a quiet corner of the multi-trillion-dollar AI industry prior to Amodei's proposal. But as concerns have mounted over whether AI companies can safeguard their models, evaluators have taken on outsized importance.
President Donald Trump encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented in late September. Anthropic's Amodei signed the accord, as did top executives at Google, Meta, OpenAI, SpaceX and Nvidia.
"We're embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same," Anthropic said Thursday.
Anthropic is developing three tiers for evaluators that grant varying levels of access to the company and its resources. First-tier evaluators will be able to conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations, second-tier evaluators can publish reports without Anthropic's approval and third-tier evaluators have employee-like access, according to a release.
METR is considered a third-tier evaluator, Anthropic said. The company has onboarded six employees from the organization, and they have access to Anthropic hardware, office spaces and tools that are "roughly on par" with what its own risk assessment teams have. The METR employees will analyze Anthropic's risk levels, incidents and practices, and publish their findings. Anthropic is not funding METR's work, according to the company.
SecureBio is considered a first-tier evaluator, Anthropic said, so its access is more limited. The organization is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons section of the risk report that it released in August. SecureBio could participate in projects with broader access and publication rights in the future.
It's not clear what level of access other organizations like Hugging Face could be granted. Hugging Face is best known for operating an open-source developer platform, and the company was thrust into the spotlight in July, when two of OpenAI's models escaped containment and gained access to Hugging Face systems through the open web. Nvidia acquired Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion last month.
Anthropic said Thursday that it's "working toward an ambitious partnership" with Accenture, but it didn't disclose how that company fits into its tiered system. Anthropic said last month that it would fund Accenture's work directly "given the importance and urgency of this work," prompting critics to raise concerns about its independence on social media.
"There are, as yet, no standards for what information embedded evaluators should have access to, or how they should report what they find. There is also no settled system for funding independent evaluation," Anthropic said in a release at the time. "Long-term, we think funding should come from pooled or government sources, as we called for in our Advanced AI Framework in June. As neither exists today, we plan to work with different evaluators under different funding arrangements."

articles.title: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
articles.text:
Porsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.
The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen-controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.
Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.
The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.
"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."
Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.
The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.
During Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track.
Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.
The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

articles.title: Retirees can take these steps to shore up income as yields rise and some dividend-paying sectors slip
articles.text: A runup in Treasury yields lately has retirees facing price declines from their bonds as well as in some of their favorite dividend-paying sectors. In the past month, the real estate and financial sectors have fallen more than 2%, while utilities are hanging in with a 1% rise and health care has risen 4%. The Vanguard High Dividend Yield Index (VYM) has fallen 1% in the past month, too. In the same period, the 10-year Treasury yield has topped 5.3%, the highest level in 24 years. The benchmark yield cooled on Thursday, trading near 5.085% as investors bid up safety assets. Still, the recent bout of volatility is enough to worry investors who are drawing down a stream of income from their retirement savings. "With fluctuations in the bond markets, I get calls from clients I don't normally hear from," said Jessica Ness, CFP and financial advisor at CJM Wealth Advisers in Falls Church, Virginia. "Any time the bond market is in turmoil, it raises clients' eyebrows," Ness added. "But it's been wonderful to say, 'no we don't need to change your strategy' or 'we don't need to adjust because your diversified portfolios have held up.'" You may not need to throw out your playbook if you're drawing down income in retirement and facing market tumult, but a few steps can help you bolster your plan. Set aside sufficient cash The best way to avoid eroding your savings during a big sell-off is to have enough cash in reserves to manage your expenses, and required withdrawals, for a six to 12-month period. Today's higher yields can also reward you with interest income from your cash without subjecting you to excessive interest rate risk. Fixed income assets with short maturities have less price sensitivity to interest rate swings; that's known as duration. The Crane 100 Money Fund Index has an annualized 7-day yield of 3.7%. Money market funds promise stability and offer interest. The Vanguard Federal Money Market Fund (VMFXX) yields 3.81% and has an expense ratio of 0.11%, while the Fidelity Money Market Fund (SPRXX) yields 3.57% and carries an expense ratio of 0.42%. For investors willing to squeeze a little more yield without ramping up duration, short-term bond funds might do the trick. The iShares Ultra Short Duration Bond Active ETF (ICSH) has an expense ratio of 0.08% and a 30-day SEC yield of 4.38%, while the Vanguard Ultra-Short Bond ETF (VUSB) has an expense ratio of 0.1% and a 30-day SEC yield of 4.78%. "We always believe in the prudence of having some cash tiering, some short-term liquidity buckets so you own an allocation that will be stable, defensive and liquid, and that you can draw down from in the most volatile markets," said Rebecca Venter, senior fixed income client portfolio manager at Vanguard. "The short-term bond space provides meaningful yield with less interest rate risk so bond portfolios can be more stable through interest rate volatility," she added. Rebalance your portfolio Don't be afraid to add back to some of your asset classes that haven't been doing well and part ways with some of your winners. Rebalancing your portfolio helps you prevent overconcentration in positions that have grown too large, keeping your risk profile in check. "Rebalancing is where the magic happens, that is where we see the opportunities," said Ness. "For us, we're trimming large cap growth; they're the high flyer." She's also been adding to some underperforming asset classes as of late, including small and mid-cap stocks. The Russell 2000 , up more than 10% in 2026, has lagged the market lately and fallen more than 7% in the past three months. The State Street SPDR S & P Midcap 400 (MDY) is off almost 4% in the past three months. Sell losers selectively If you're holding bonds in your taxable brokerage account, the latest runup in yields may have given you an opportunity to sell a few losing positions to offset capital gains realized elsewhere in your portfolio. If your losses exceed capital gains, you can apply as much as $3,000 of the losses to reduce your ordinary income. You can also carry over any unused losses into future years. But investors need to steer clear of violating the wash sale rule. That means if you sell an asset to realize a loss and then buy a "substantially identical" replacement within 30 days before or after the transaction, the IRS may stop you from taking the loss. "This is a great time for [tax loss harvesting on bonds], and I think for clients who are in higher tax brackets, the taxable equivalent yield on municipal bonds is really attractive," said Rafia Hasan, CFP and chief investment officer at Perigon Wealth Management in Chicago. She recommends shying away from bonds with very long duration, instead preferring intermediate duration – somewhere in the range of five to seven years. Hasan noted that while it's a tough market for fixed income, yield is now making up a larger part of total bond returns. "On a go-forward basis, it's a positive for people who are savers and bond investors," she said.

articles.title: Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now
articles.text:
POWER POINT
What I'm hearing from energy insiders
Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.
That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.
Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out. If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.
As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.
Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.
I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.
You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.
***
On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.
The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.
Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.
Brian
THE ACTIONABLE INSIDER
The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.
Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.
Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."
Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.
Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.
In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.
The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).
Fun Fact → While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.
Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.
First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.
Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.
TAKE A LOOK
In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.
INSIDE LINE
RANDOM, BUT INTERESTING
The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.
The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.
Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.
THE GRID
Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
Iran says it's 'counting the moments' until it can strike U.S. warships

articles.title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
articles.text:
KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

articles.title: Nvidia and Cisco confirm multimillion-dollar donations to Trump's White House ballroom
articles.text:
Technology giants Nvidia and Cisco have committed millions to President Donald Trump's White House ballroom renovation project, CNBC confirmed on Thursday.
Nvidia and Apple each pledged $25 million to the project, according to a report from The Washington Post. Those were among the largest donations on the list, which totaled more than $330 million.
"As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," an Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made."
Amazon, Palantir, ServiceNow, Meta Platforms and Microsoft also made contributions in the millions, according to the Post. Microsoft and Meta declined to comment on the report. Cisco and ServiceNow confirmed their $5 million donation.
"ServiceNow's business with the U.S. government is separate and unconnected to any donations we make to any cause," the company said in a statement to CNBC. "Any attempt to connect the two processes is wholly inaccurate."
Amazon, Apple, HP Inc., Micron, Palantir, Salesforce and Vast Space, which were all listed as major donors in the report, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Post reported that the ballroom donations were sent through a nonprofit trust, and donors received a pledge form for donating to the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom."
Lawmakers and experts have repeatedly called out donations to the project, requesting information on the private donors. Some have also raised concerns over the potential influence these commitments could have on policy decisions or any federal contract awards.
Tech leaders have largely favored Trump's pro-business, light-touch approach to antitrust and regulation, and some companies have secured hundreds of millions in contracts through artificial intelligence infrastructure and defense deals during his second term.
Tech leaders like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have been regulars at state dinners and meetings in Washington, and were central figures at the White House AI luncheon on Sept. 29.
The documents obtained by the Post showed 67 contributions above $10,000 as of late September.
Read the full story from The Washington Post here.

articles.title: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% in fiscal 2026, lifted by SpaceX as top holding
articles.text:
Harvard University's endowment grew 27.1% in fiscal year 2026, its strongest return in five years, the school said in its annual financial report released on Thursday.
The endowment, which beat the S&P 500's 22.3% total return in the same period by 4.8 percentage points, now totals nearly $68 billion. The outperformance came amid actions by the Trump administration to penalize the school and withhold funding from the university.
"While markets can easily take back what they give, that return will strengthen the endowment's capacity to support the University over time," Harvard's chief financial officer Ritu Kalra and treasurer Timothy Barakett wrote in the 49-page annual report. "The University deliberately smooths distributions so that operating support does not rise and fall with the markets. Strong investment returns therefore support Harvard's work gradually, through future distributions."
The returns marked the best year for the endowment, managed by the Harvard Management Company, since 2021. Harvard's fiscal year ends on June 30.
In its second-quarter 13F filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Harvard unveiled a $2.2 billion stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX rocket and satellite company. It marked the endowment's largest single holding by value, trailed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at just under $350 million.
Harvard's financial picture, though, is undermined by moves by the federal government. Federally-sponsored research revenue declined 19.5% to $509 million in fiscal 2026.
And starting in the current fiscal year, "endowment resources will face an additional constraint, with the federal excise tax on Harvard's net investment income rising nearly six-fold, from 1.4% to 8%," Kalra and Barakett wrote. "We estimate the higher rate will cost roughly $300 million a year."
"[I]n a year of returns like this one," the federal excise tax "would be several times larger," they noted.
President Alan Garber acknowledged such headwinds, but said in the report that Harvard can still succeed.
"Together, we have the opportunity to set the University on a path to excellence that none of us can imagine today," he said. "Notwithstanding the challenges and uncertainty, this is a thrilling time to be part of a great American institution devoted to Veritas."

articles.title: Some 'classic' money advice is actually pretty new—and not all of it is worthwhile, says historian
articles.text:
In the world of personal finance, many of the lessons we're taught are touted as historical. Since the dawn of time, the experts tell us, those who got ahead financially lived within their means, saved diligently and spent and invested carefully.
It made Joseph Moore — a historian and author of "How to Get Rich in American History," published in April — wonder if Americans had been receiving, following and prospering from the same advice for the past few centuries. What he found surprised him.
"Is there timeless wisdom of money that we should all be following, from Ben Franklin to now? The answer is no," Moore says. "It turns out, what 'always' worked is always changing."
Some common financial principles that seem old are recent phenomena, Moore says, and some situations that seem new are, in fact, quite common throughout history.
In both such cases, knowing your history can be helpful. After all, if previous generations flourished without more recent advice, maybe the current wisdom isn't as valuable as we think. Conversely, maybe you don't need to find a creative solution to a problem that isn't actually that novel.
Here are three misconceptions Moore points out from the history of American personal finance — and what you can learn from them.
Housing shortages aren't new
Americans are struggling with housing affordability amid high mortgage rates and rising home prices. But it's not a historically unique problem, Moore says.
"We absolutely are in a housing crisis caused by a housing shortage," he says. "It's neither the first nor the worst."
Moore points to 1948, when the ratio of people who wanted to buy a house to available inventory was about double what it is now, as the worst culprit. The year 1981, when the median new mortgage consumed more than half of the median household income, was no picnic either, he says.
That doesn't mean that the current shortage isn't real or that you should suck it up because other people had it worse, Moore says.
But it is worth looking at how people have historically solved it — personally, not politically. And in the case of a housing shortage, Moore's answers aren't glamorous.
One historical solution was moving more often. Currently, the housing market is worse in some places than others. Folks used to be more likely to pick up and go to places where opportunities were better, Moore says. For most of the country's history, between 1 in 3 and 1 in 5 Americans moved every year, he says, pointing to research by historian and journalist Yoni Appelbaum. Now, it's more like 1 in 13, Moore notes.
Another common solution for unaffordable homes: sharing housing. In 19th-century America, it wasn't at all uncommon for homeowners to rent out rooms in their house to help with the mortgage, Moore says. The same logic applies to modern-day renters who split spaces with roommates to keep costs down, he says.
"It's a shortage of space, so you have to monetize space," says Moore.
Diversification and compounding weren't the historical path to wealth
Investors are often told that the path to long-term wealth is simple: Invest consistently in a low-cost, broadly diversified stock portfolio. Need proof? Consider the S&P 500's upward trajectory since before the stock market crash in 1929, and think of all the compounding returns you could have earned over that period had you invested.
"Something really new that we act like is really old is that compound interest is what builds wealth," Moore says. "Nobody got rich by compound interest for most of U.S. history, and if they did, they were generally already wealthy."
Think about it: Index funds weren't around, nor were fractional shares. If you wanted to own every stock in an index, you'd need to have the money to buy shares of each, plus a fee for your broker, of course.
"For most of American history, less than 10% of Americans owned stocks at all. That's not how people got wealthy," Moore says. "They got wealthy by concentrating most of their efforts in small businesses and careers, real estate and job tools. [Few people] compounded their way to wealth until the greatest generation and baby boomers, when the technology came online to allow you to use compounding."
Investors should still take advantage of the innovations that made diversified, low-cost portfolios widely accessible, Moore says. Just remember that there's more than one way to build wealth.
People used to keep budgeting simple
One piece of financial advice that feels tried and true is to create a budget and stick to it. How else can you make sure you don't overspend and keep yourself on track toward your financial goals?
But Moore says that the household spending spreadsheet is a relatively new phenomenon.
"Nobody in the 1800s budgeted the way we talk about budgeting," he says. "These forward-facing spending categories would be completely foreign to anyone's thinking."
For most of American history, what folks did instead was look at their money in big buckets. A couple might divide things between the husband's and wife's income, for instance, he says. Or, to keep things even simpler, they divided income between what they needed to survive, and whatever was leftover.
More complex budgeting schemes came into fashion in the early 20th century, Moore says, with financial guides at the time touting how much you could save by slashing the likes of alcohol and tobacco — the lattes and avocado toast of their day.
There's no one right way to manage money. But if you find budgeting tedious, Moore argues that attitude puts you in line with generations of Americans who kept things simple by practicing what we'd now call reverse budgeting: paying their bills, putting money away for goals and then spending the rest as they saw fit.

articles.title: Here's our monthly update on our 32 stocks, including 2 more names to buy
articles.text: What a week to have a Monthly Meeting. On Thursday, Jim Cramer and portfolio director Jeff Marks held our October Monthly Meeting. They ran through our portfolio during this cloudy moment for the AI trade. Nevertheless, as Jim explained to start the meeting, we have faith "the sun will come out again." Jim called out Goldman Sachs and Starbucks as his two favorite stocks to buy right now (we also bought Bank of New York before the meeting began). Note: Jim and Jeff didn't have a chance to talk about Johnson & Johnson during the meeting, though our latest thinking on the healthcare giant is included below. Tech and AI stocks Apple : The iPhone maker is defying the AI sell-off and trading at all-time highs. That seems like an oddity, but remember it's not spending tens of billions on data center capital expenditures. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin Friday (and the foldable phone hits the shelves next week). We think this will be a big hit. Broadcom : This is a tough one, maybe the toughest. While we slashed the position in August ahead of earnings, its reliance on Anthropic and OpenAI as custom-chip customers makes us wish we had exited it altogether. As long as AI financing concerns are in question, Broadcom's stock may struggle to rally, and we're marking this one for sale. Intel : We're steadfast that the chipmaker will be a winner in the AI era, thanks to both the renaissance in central processing units (CPUs) and the need for a manufacturing alternative to TSMC . But we're holding off on buying more until the low $80s. It is difficult to buy more in this neighborhood when price-to-earnings multiples are compressing. Micron : Speaking of P/E valuations, one of our reasons for buying this memory-chip maker was a belief that steadier earnings in the AI cycle would be rewarded with a higher multiple. At this point, we still think the earnings will come through, and a voracious buyback looms in December. It's just harder to count on that multiple expansion when the AI trade is on the ropes. Qnity : The DuPont spin-off that supplies materials used to make semiconductors remains an under-the-radar play on the AI boom. As Qnity gets discovered, we think it will be regarded as inexpensive versus its peers. This special-situation status keeps us invested. If you haven't yet, check out our inside look at one of Qnity's facilities outside Boston. The company gave us a rare, in-depth look at its operations. Eaton and GE Vernova : We've made excellent money in these two industrials levered to the data center buildout. Nevertheless, in this moment, we recognize the stocks could fall much lower if there is, in fact, debt problems among the data center builders. The counterbalance is both Eaton and GE Vernova stand to benefit from the electric grid overhaul that needs to happen, irrespective of AI. Alphabet : The Google parent needs to make its Gemini AI assistant more competitive versus Anthropic, OpenAI, and now Meta, but it is a stock we would look to buy more of as it goes down, not sell. The Google Cloud and YouTube businesses are just cash machines. Meta Platforms : The first of three hard-fought tech victories, Meta is back in Wall Street's good graces thanks to the remarkably successful launch of its Muse personal agent app. Nobody has Muse in their earnings estimates, so the numbers are probably too low. While Meta may have to spend more on data centers to support Muse, we think it has a responsible approach. Microsoft : The second hard-fought winner, Microsoft was even tougher to hold than Meta. Yet it clawed its way back and on Tuesday notched its first record close in almost a year . The Street was convinced Microsoft had nothing to offer in the AI world. We trusted management to figure it out, and now Copilot has momentum and growth for its Azure cloud business is accelerating. Salesforce : Rounding out the trio of tech names we had to battle is Salesforce. Not only has CEO Marc Benioff built a compelling agentic AI offering with Agentforce, but he used the "SaaSpocalypse" panic to buy back a bunch of stock at much lower prices in March. The stock still looks cheap, trading at a mid-teens multiple on forward earnings estimates, which should help shares grind higher. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks : Cybersecurity remains an important industry to have exposure to because companies need sturdy defenses to prevent agents from going rogue. At the same time, we recognize these stocks have had major moves and people are probably sitting on big profits. We've taken some off the table ourselves and can't fault anyone for doing the same. Nvidia : While we understand some people may be concerned with all of Nvidia's investments into other companies across the AI ecosystem, afraid of "circularity," we still want to bank on CEO Jensen Huang. He has a crystal-clear vision of where the AI revolution is going. Still an "own it, don't trade it" name. Amazon : If the e-commerce giant can demonstrate that its massive AI investments are starting to generate profits on its next earnings call while signaling that capital expenditure growth is beginning to moderate, expect shares to take off. We have tremendous confidence in CEO Andy Jassy and CFO Brian Olsavsky, and if we didn't own any of the stock here, we would buy some. The financials Goldman Sachs : The investment bank delivered the strongest quarter of any financial company so far this earnings season, yet shares are still down big from their highs of the summer and trade at just 12 times earnings. We see that as an attractive buying opportunity. Goldman is also well positioned to capitalize on the market volatility fueled by higher interest rates, while an eventual end to the Iran war could unleash another wave of mergers and acquisitions and IPOs. Wells Fargo : Another imperfect quarter was frustrating, but that's no reason to give up on a bank trading at just 11 times earnings and run by the incredibly smart Charlie Scharf. The CEO has been expanding Wells Fargo's investment banking and credit card businesses, creating new opportunities for growth. Scharf also recently indicated that the bank stands to benefit from higher interest rates. BNY : No doubt our initiation in early September was poorly timed, but we still have tremendous faith in CEO Robin Vince. Earlier Thursday, the bank beat Wall Street expectations on both revenue and earnings. BNY's numbers looked particularly good compared with rival State Street's disappointing results a day earlier. We took advantage of the weakness to add to our position Thursday morning. Capital One : The credit-card issuer's stock is very sensitive to the economy and gasoline prices, so that's been a headwind and explains some of the underperformance. We understand the pain. But we still believe in the Discover acquisition being lucrative, and with shares trading at less than 10 times earnings, we're holding on. The remaining names Linde : The industrial gas giant delivered a fine quarter in late July, supported by steady growth in its relatively defensive business (though healthcare was a blemish). We continue to like Linde's ability to perform even when the broader industrial economy faces cyclical pressures. DuPont : The chemicals company delivered a terrific quarter in August considering challenges facing its clean-water business in the Middle East, but we're keeping the stock on a short leash in the face of rate hikes and higher oil prices. Its exposure to the cyclical construction market remains a concern, and the breakup catalyst has largely played out. Need another reason to own the stock beyond the restructuring, like some M & A. Cardinal Health : Want a perfect stock for this nervous market? How about a drug distributor transforming into a higher-growth specialty healthcare provider? That's Cardinal, which is why the stock has had such a big move this month. As much as we like the story, we don't want to get greedy, so we trimmed our position Thursday morning at $251. We had bought 50 shares at $223 apiece on Sept. 30. Eli Lilly : Shares are jumping Thursday as part of the market's rotation into defensive names. At current levels above $1,200, we're closer to booking profits than we are adding to the position. Still, the company has the best obesity pipeline and the best scale. Oral obesity drug Foundayo is gaining ground on Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill. Johnson & Johnson : The stock has been benefiting from the same rotation as Lilly, though off the day's highs. The biggest problem in its quarterly results Tuesday was the cardiovascular unit within its MedTech segment, though management insists the problems are fixable. While not ideal, we love the way its pharmaceutical business is performing and expect continued growth ahead. Costco : Although the warehouse retailer's membership renewal rate had wobbled, particularly among younger shoppers who shop more online, its earnings report on Sept. 24 showed improvements. Still, at roughly 42 times earnings, the stock is about as expensive as we're willing to tolerate in a rising rate environment. Further upside will need to come from earnings growth rather than multiple expansion. The good news is we're confident Costco can deliver that. TJX Companies : The off-price retailer's recent stumble may have reflected complacency after years of dominance, particularly as Ross Stores has become a tougher competitor under new CEO Jim Conroy. We're optimistic that TJX is getting back on track . Shares have rallied sharply since we bought in late August and mid-September near their lows. Thanks to those well-timed buys, we'd look to take some profits at these levels if our trading restrictions allowed. Starbucks : CEO Brian Niccol's turnaround is gaining momentum, and the coffee chain may be taking market share from competitors. Niccol personally assured us that Starbucks isn't pursuing a Chipotle acquisition, and that the encouraging trends from its latest quarter are continuing. Stronger earnings can drive the stock higher without multiple expansion. Other than Goldman Sachs, Starbucks is the stock we're most eager to buy. FedEx Freight : The less-than-truckload shipping company continues to struggle as elevated diesel prices weigh on shares. While we're tempted by this pullback, we're reluctant to increase our exposure to trucking stocks amid the uncertainty. We'll look to J.B. Hunt's earnings Thursday night for a better read on the broader freight market before making any moves. FedEx Corp : The shipping giant is one of the most undervalued stocks in the portfolio, as CEO Raj Subramaniam continues to improve efficiency and strengthen its competitive position. While we're eager to buy more shares at these levels, we're staying disciplined given the challenging market environment. Boeing : We're sticking with the planemaker despite the stock's recent weakness. CEO Kelly Ortberg continues to make progress, with Boeing recently averting a strike and securing a $20 billion defense contract. Regulators also determined that a software glitch reported in September did not pose a flight safety risk. Yet shares have continued to fall, largely because higher oil prices are weighing on aerospace stocks. Kimberly-Clark : The Huggies parent delivered some much-needed good news earlier Thursday, reporting preliminary third-quarter results ahead of expectations and reaffirming its full-year outlook. Chinese authorities also said no toxic substances were found in its products, disproving social-media claims that previously hurt sales . While its acquisition of Kenvue still needs approval in Brazil, we see this deal as a major catalyst, with Kimberly-Clark capable of getting more out of the Band-Aid and Tylenol parent than when it was part of Johnson & Johnson and as a standalone company. articles.title: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
articles.text:
Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter, his campaign announced Thursday, setting what the campaign said is a Senate fundraising record as Republicans pour outside money into the race to bolster GOP nominee Ken Paxton in the 2026 midterm election.
The haul was the largest ever reported by a Senate candidate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the campaign, surpassing the previous record of $57 million set by South Carolina Democrat Jaime Harrison, who unsuccessfully ran against Republican Lindsey Graham in 2020.
Talarico has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year, according to his campaign ahead of the quarterly filing deadline with the Federal Election Commission.
“Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement.
The campaign said more than 1.3 million people have donated and that 97% of contributions were $100 or less. Paxton, by comparison, announced earlier this month that his campaign and two affiliated fundraising committees raised a combined $18 million during the quarter.
The candidates' full financial picture will become clearer after their quarterly reports are filed with the FEC. The filings will show how much each campaign spent and how much cash they had left entering the final stretch.
But the gap in direct fundraising tells only part of the financial story. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million since Sept. 1 supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico, according to AdImpact, helping offset Paxton's weaker campaign fundraising. Overall political advertising in the race has surpassed $500 million.
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has emerged as a major force in the race, giving $10 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC, according to figures confirmed Monday by a spokesman for Musk's America PAC, while his America PAC has spent about $9.4 million attacking Talarico and another $1.8 million supporting Paxton, according to FEC filings.
The source of that money matters as federal law guarantees candidates lower broadcast rates for television advertising than super PACs, allowing Talarico's campaign dollars to go further in buying TV exposure than outside Republican groups.
No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a U.S. Senate race there since 1988. But Talarico leads Paxton 48.5% to 45.2% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average, a 3.3-percentage point advantage, forcing Republicans to devote significant resources to what has traditionally been safe territory.
Talarico's fundraising also eclipses previous high-water marks for Texas Democrats. Beto O'Rourke raised $38.1 million in the third quarter of 2018 during his challenge to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

articles.title: This semiconductor stock is not for the faint of heart. Here's why I see opportunity
articles.text: Lam Research Corporation has been on an impressive run this year, but with shares pulling back from their highs, I see an attractive buying opportunity. We already own in our Mango Growth ETF and we're looking to potentially add to our position following the recent sell-off. The Fremont-based company makes specialized equipment that chipmakers use to manufacture semiconductors. Its tools help create the tiny, intricate structures inside advanced chips, making Lam an important supplier to the companies powering the artificial intelligence boom. Key points AI spending is driving demand for the advanced chips that Lam's equipment helps manufacture. As chips become more sophisticated, Lam's technology is becoming more essential to their production. Growing services business provides steady revenue and a cushion against a slowdown in AI spending. Lam is an important part of the semiconductor supply chain, even if it doesn't get the same attention as the companies designing AI chips. And as the industry works to make chips more powerful and efficient, I believe Lam's equipment will become increasingly valuable. Why I'm buying AI spending continues to fuel demand The world's largest technology companies are spending heavily on AI infrastructure, driving demand for more advanced chips and memory. Lam reported record June-quarter revenue of $6.72 billion , up 30% from a year earlier. Revenue tied to NAND memory, used for data storage, more than doubled from the previous quarter. That momentum is expected to continue. Management projected September-quarter revenue of $8.1 billion and expects its advanced chip packaging business to grow more than 70% in 2026. I believe there's plenty of room for further growth. More complex chips mean more opportunities for Lam As semiconductors become more complex, manufacturers increasingly rely on Lam's specialized equipment. The company specializes in etching and deposition, two essential manufacturing processes. Put simply, its machines carve intricate patterns into chips and add the extremely thin layers needed to build them. I think the growing complexity of advanced chips presents a significant growth opportunity for Lam. Its services business offers protection against a slowdown Lam also generates revenue by servicing and upgrading machines already installed in customers' factories. That business is growing rapidly, with revenue from its Customer Support Business Group climbing more than 40% year over year in the second quarter. LRCX YTD mountain Lam Research Corporation, YTD I like that this is a high-margin business with a more dependable revenue stream than new equipment sales. It could help cushion Lam if major technology companies eventually slow their AI spending. Why now? After a strong run earlier this year, Lam shares have pulled back roughly 37% from their 52-week high of $438.50 to around $275. I see this as an attractive buying opportunity following some profit-taking, particularly with earnings coming up on Oct. 21. Lam has beaten earnings estimates for 12 consecutive quarters, and its strong fundamentals could support another solid report. Bottom line Lam Research looks well positioned to benefit as AI chips become increasingly sophisticated and demand for its specialized equipment grows. The stock isn't for the faint of heart. Investors should be prepared for continued volatility, but I'm willing to ride it out given the long-term opportunity. Jeff Kilburg is the founder and CEO of KKM Financial. Prior to starting his own firm, he spent more than two decades on the floors of the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) and Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE). articles.title: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
articles.text:
Tesla is planning to show off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car.
The event will be livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. It's expected to begin at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET.
Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.
The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology, such as cold gas thrusters, to enable it to hover. Musk fanatics have been gearing up for the demonstration, expressing their excitement on social media, but the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.
Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Executives are expected to disclose specific pricing, details and production targets.
Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017, and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."
Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either.
Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his own reservation and refund requests.
"I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait."
Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure.
Others have kept their reservations.
Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000.
O'Connor wrote in a message that he plans to attend Thursday's event and is "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making."
According to filings with the Federal Aviation Administration, Tesla established a no-fly zone around the SpaceX facility where it plans to show off the vehicle. The company had to scrap a demo on Oct. 1 due to weather issues.
Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

articles.title: BNY stock pops on strong earnings — showing exactly why we like this bank in this market
articles.text: Bank of New York on Thursday delivered top- and bottom-line beats, with better-than-expected fee-based revenue and net interest income, as well as healthy pre-tax margin expansion. The strength of the quarter set the stage for management to boost full-year guidance. Revenue in the third quarter rose 12% year over year to $5.7 billion, ahead of the $5.5 billion consensus, according to the analyst estimates compiled by data provider LSEG. This marks BNY's 15th consecutive quarter of year-over-year revenue growth. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) in the three months ended Sept. 30 jumped 24% to $2.37, which excludes a 3-cent-per-share severance expense, versus the $2.27 expected, according to LSEG data. Bottom Line Wall Street clearly liked what it heard on the post-earnings conference call because BNY stock went from flat to up more than 3% on the day. While it could always get swept lower given this week's brutal sell-off on AI funding and midterm fears, we think the results point to any weakness as a buying opportunity for those able to stomach increased volatility between now and the next month's elections, which is why we opted to step in and pick up a few more shares Thursday morning. We are reiterating our buy-equivalent 1 rating and $180 price target. BNY YTD mountain Bank of New York YTD BNY may not be the largest bank in the world by revenue, but it is the largest custodian bank in the world. While it may manage only about $2 trillion in assets, it is in charge of safeguarding more than $60 trillion worth of assets. Managed assets are those for which BNY has decision-making power, such as portfolio structure, asset allocation, and so on. For assets under custody, BNY acts as a protector with administrative responsibilities. In both cases, BNY generates fees. However, fees generated from managed assets are tied to market fluctuations, making them more volatile, while those tied to the much larger custodian business tend to be far more stable. When initiating BNY on Sept. 2, we highlighted the bank's heavily fee-based business model as an attractive diversifier versus the deposits and loans focus of Wells Fargo and the investment banking and wealth management focus at Goldman Sachs. Assets under custody/administration increased 10% thanks to an increase in market values, net client inflows, and net new business. As a result, BNY delivered the fee-based revenue results we were looking for, even as a 2% year-over-year increase in assets under management was a tad less than the Street was looking for. Fee-based revenues outpaced expectations, growing 12% year over year on strength pretty much across the board. The team attributed the growth to "net new business, higher client activity and higher market values," partially offset by the mix of assets under management (AUM) flows. Quarterly commentary Net-interest income (NII) was also better than expected, increasing 15% versus the year-ago period as investment securities were reinvested at higher yields and the balance sheet grew. While BNY's Tangible Book Value Per Share (TBVPS) did come up a bit short of expectations, a better-than-expected Return on Tangible Common Equity (ROTCE) served as an offset. These two metrics are key factors in determining the appropriate multiple on which to value financial firms. BNY's Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) Ratio came in at 10.9%, a bit below expectations. However, it was well above the Federal Reserve's 8.5% enforced minimum, providing plenty of capacity for growth-oriented investments and shareholder returns. During the quarter, BNY returned a total of $1.4 billion to shareholders, with about two-thirds coming from buybacks and the remainder from dividend payments, resulting in a year-to-date payout ratio (dividends divided by net income) of 86%. BNY has three key operating segments: (1) Securities services, which cater to asset owners, managers, and corporate clients; (2) Market and Wealth services, which address the needs of financial institutions, corporations, foundations and endowments, public funds, and government agencies; and (3) Investment and Wealth Management — unlike the first two, which generate custodial fees — is the segment that houses the assets that BNY is actually responsible for managing. Securities services delivered 15% year-on-year revenue growth, as 12% growth in asset servicing was compounded by a 27% increase in issuer services. Market and Wealth services revenue was up nearly 12% versus the year-ago period, with revenue generated from wealth solutions increasing 10%, payments and trade revenue increasing 14%, and revenue from clearance and collateral management increasing 12% year over year. Investment and Wealth Management realized 4% revenue growth year over year, with investment management revenue increasing 1% and wealth management revenue increasing 11% year over year. Guidance Looking ahead, here are the details on management's outlook raise. Total revenue growth is now expected to increase about 12% to 13% (market dependent), better than the 11% growth expected coming into the print. Helping to drive that top-line growth, the team expects NII to be up 15% year-over-year, ahead of the 14% growth expected, according to FactSet. Given the increased revenue outlook, revenue-related expenses are also expected to increase a bit more than expected. That's of course acceptable given the raised expense outlook is tied into the increased revenue outlook. Importantly, the team also adjusted guidance for operating leverage (calculated as the rate of increase in revenue less the rate of increase in noninterest expense), increasing it by about 500 basis points, up from the roughly 400 basis points increase forecast last quarter and well above the 100 basis point guide at the start of the year. articles.title: Here are the stocks reporting next week that have a history of earnings beats and big share gains
articles.text: A handful of companies reporting earnings soon have a strong history of not only surpassing Wall Street's expectations, but also rewarding investors with a jump in shares following their results. Earnings season continues next week, with companies across technology, financials, industrials and consumer sectors set to post their latest quarterly results. Household products maker Procter & Gamble and railroad shipper Union Pacific are among those slated to report. CNBC Pro screened data from Bespoke Investment Group for companies posting results next week that have beaten earnings-per-share estimates at least 80% of the time and whose shares have gained an average of 1.5% or more on earnings days. The screen turned up seven stocks, including RingCentral , Intuitive Surgical and Deckers Outdoor . RingCentral has the strongest historical record on the screen. The cloud communications company topped estimates 98% of the time, while its shares have posted an average gain of 4.2% on earnings day, the largest among the companies on the list. RingCentral is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the closing bell on Oct. 22. The company recently entered a strategic partnership with Allnet.Italia, an information and communications technology firm. The alliance will enable Allnet.Italia's network of channel partners to sell, implement and support advanced AI offerings in the Italian market, according to a statement. "With RingCentral, we now complete that portfolio with an AI-first cloud platform, giving resellers a way to build recurring revenue on a proven global platform, backed by our local team from pre-sales to deployment," said Emiliano Papadopoulos, CEO of Allnet.Italia in a statement. Shares are up 160% this year. Analysts polled by LSEG largely rate RingCentral hold, and consensus price targets suggest the stock could slip 27% from current levels. Intuitive Surgical also emerged on the list. The robotic surgery company has beaten earnings estimates 89% of the time and averaged a 2.4% gain on earnings days. Shares of Intuitive Surgical fell more than 1% Tuesday alongside other medical-device stocks after Johnson & Johnson reported weaker-than-expected MedTech sales. Intuitive Surgical is expected to report on Oct. 20. In all, 25 out of 35 analysts rate the stock a buy or strong buy, and consensus price targets suggest almost 15% upside, per LSEG. Intuitive Surgical is down nearly 26% in 2026.

articles.title: Anduril CEO defends Trump administration contracts: 'We've done incredibly well under Biden'
articles.text:
Anduril CEO Brian Schimpf addressed ethics questions over co-founder Palmer Luckey's close ties to the Trump administration as the defense tech giant competes for lucrative government contracts.
"We've done incredibly well under [President Joe] Biden," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "That was one of the biggest ramps that we've had as a company. I'm a lifelong Dem and have great relationships on both sides of the aisle of this."
On Oct. 6, Anduril announced an up to $2.9 billion shipyard contract a few days after Luckey was named to a Department of Defense group known as Project Meridian. The company also won a multi-year DOD contract worth up to $20 billion in March.
The appointments of both Luckey and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to the initiative have raised concerns over whether executives whose companies get billions in government contracts should play an active role in defense strategy.
"The reality is that the [Department of Defense] has just an incredibly structured process for how they evaluate all these incoming bids," Schimpf said. "So everything goes through these very competitive processes, and we win based on the merits."
Musk has contributed more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, CNBC reported this week. Luckey, who helped raise money for President Donald Trump's 2020 campaign, has donated more than $500,000 to Republican candidates and GOP-aligned groups this year, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.
This week, Anduril opened a tender offer to employees in 16 countries that would value the company at $90 billion, five months after it topped a $60 billion valuation.
Schimpf said the setup allows Anduril to give liquidity to employees without the distraction of stock price fluctuations. Like Anthropic, OpenAI and Databricks, Anduril has benefitted from an abundance of private market funding opportunities that have allowed businesses to extend the timeline to any public offering.
Luckey has voiced his intentions to eventually take the California-based company public. Schimpf told CNBC in July that Anduril isn't rushing into an IPO, adding that "a bad time" to debut is during a hype cycle.
"This allows us to stay really focused on what we need to do – which is a massive, unprecedented ramp in defense production that we need to execute on over the next couple of years," Schimpf told CNBC on Thursday, referring to the employee tender offer.
Anduril was founded in 2017 to disrupt the traditional defense contractor space. Over the years, the company gained a reputation for its autonomous unmanned devices, drone boats and software it supplies to the U.S. Department of Defense and allied militaries.
The company is also among a growing number of defense startups deploying their systems overseas, including the Middle East, as the U.S. government seeks to expand next-gen capabilities.
The use of these new artificial intelligence-equipped systems has also drawn ethics concerns and questions about human intervention. Anthropic's recent spat with the Pentagon stemmed from a disagreement over the use of its models in military conflict.
"Fundamentally, anytime you are making critical decisions about use of force or how to employ these, or what the consequences are of your actions, that is fundamentally a human decision," Schimpf told CNBC.
—CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article.

articles.title: How to get the best prices online—and fight back against companies that experiment on shoppers
articles.text:
Shopping should not be both increasingly expensive and increasingly exhausting.
I've worked as an economic sociologist and consumer advocate for over a decade and helped craft policies on Capitol Hill to protect American shoppers. I'm currently the president and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a think tank and advocacy group focused on making the economy more accessible to everyone.
In my new book, "Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet," I delve into unfair practices like surveillance pricing — essentially when companies offer you and your friend, for example, two different prices for the same product based on your personal information.
I believe, from the bottom of my heart, that it's not the job of the consumer alone to try to beat the machine. Battling the pricing bots isn't the future that I want for us. But I think it is time to update our rules for an age of e-commerce, agentic commerce and shopping that is increasingly assisted by artificial intelligence.
Many of the tips I suggest in my book might save you money, but they will eat up another different valuable resource: your time. With all that in mind, this is my best advice — and strategies that I personally use — for anyone who wants to get better and fairer prices when shopping online.
Uncover the hidden ways to comparison shop
It used to be that to compare the products you wanted to buy, you would look at similar stores and see what the better price point was. That's not enough anymore. There are more ways to comparison shop than you might think, and a lot of them are hiding in plain sight.
Think of any way you could possibly buy something online. Even for the same company, it's likely that the price is going to be different based on how you access it.
What are you being charged at the brick-and-mortar store versus the website versus the app? Are you logged in or logged out? How much is the item when you search on an iPhone versus an Android phone versus a laptop? How much is it when you ask a chatbot to get it for you? All of these are now sources of pricing variation.
You also might consider using a virtual private network or going into incognito mode as well. Comparison shopping more exhaustively can be just that, exhausting. But it is one of my chief recommendations if you want to be as sure as you can that you are getting the best price, even from the same store.
Turn the experiment back around on companies
Some companies experiment on you to figure out how much they can charge you. So my advice is to flip it and reverse it.
Before you buy Thanksgiving airline tickets, sit down with your spouse and see if one of you gets the better deal. If you're at a concert with friends, before you book a car to go home, all three of you should fire up the same rideshare app and see if one of you gets the lower price.
You may see prices and fees vary across people, even for the same item at the same time, or the same ride to the same destination.
My organization, Groundwork Collaborative, has conducted and collaborated on investigations that bear this out. We recently ran an experiment with NBC's "TODAY." We asked folks in the studio to open StubHub and buy the same Harry Styles concert tickets at Madison Square Garden. Fees varied across the participants.
In a statement, a spokesperson from StubHub said, "We use randomized, anonymous tests to find which discounts best balance demand and access. These pricing tests don't use data like demographics, location or purchase history."
Experimentation is really important and it's one of the key ways that we can fight back against these practices.
Use your voice to bring power back to the consumer
In "Gouged," I outline what I call a Shoppers' Bill of Rights, a comprehensive set of local, state and federal policy solutions to level the playing field between retailers and shoppers. We're not there yet, but there is a lot you can do right now to help bring some of the power back to consumers.
When you call your local lawmakers, you can say something to the effect of: "I know that there are a lot of reasons prices are high right now, and I know that you don't have a lot of control over many of them. But you can work to ban surveillance pricing, the practice of spying on you to overcharge you. You can work to eliminate junk fees and require companies to show you the full price of something up front. You can work to ensure that I can get a refund on the same card I bought the item on — without fighting a chatbot for three hours. You can help me cancel my subscriptions by making companies offer simple ways to get out of stuff."
Those are all things in the Shoppers' Bill of Rights that lawmakers can take on. And those seemingly small changes could help Americans get fairer prices.
So don't be afraid to use your own platform. If you are trying to buy something and see four different prices on four different platforms for the same store, call it out. At a minimum, post about it. I think that consumers raising their voices is an important way that we start the work of consumer advocacy and bring attention to these issues. Companies will often respond if they are worried about losing market share.
At the same time, when you do run into issues, it's important to report what you experience to local officials, whether that is an attorney general or someone involved at the state level in consumer protections.
On social media, you can certainly talk about companies that are engaging in these unfair practices, but you can also highlight the ones that are committing to go in a different direction. Shout out your favorite small business that isn't using algorithmic pricing. One of the best things you can do is support indie businesses and shop local whenever you can.
Lindsay Owens is president and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative. She is the author of "Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet" (Viking) and the Gouged newsletter.

articles.title: South Korea Unemployment Rate
articles.text:
South Korea’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 2.6% in September 2026 from 2.7% in August, reaching its lowest level since September 2024. The economy added 113,000 jobs, marking three consecutive months of gains over 100,000 and bringing total employment to 29.27 million. Human health and social work activities led job creation, adding 207,000 workers, while manufacturing rose by 16,000, its first increase since June 2024 and ending a 26-month streak of declines. In contrast, accommodation and food service employment fell by 97,000 for a second consecutive month, recording its largest decline since February 2021. Employment also fell in agriculture, forestry and fishing (-94,000) and construction (-48,000). Meanwhile, the number of unemployed people was 600,000, down 34,000 from the same month a year ago, while the economically inactive population increased by 179,000 to 16,188,000. Youth employment rate for those aged 15 to 29 was 44.0%, down 1.1 percentage points. source: Statistics Korea

articles.title: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
articles.text:
The federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.
The lawsuit is the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which President Donald Trump has often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.
The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."
The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.
Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality."
"Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.
The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.
The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County.
McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.
Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls."
"Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing."
"Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."
Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."
"My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.
Weber's office declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday, but pointed to a letter she had sent McCotter in response to his letter.
Weber, in her letter, said, "California's election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands."
She said that "despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours."
"This is an emergency of the DOJ's creation," Weber said.
