articles.title: A lot changed in stock market in just a few months. The single biggest risk did not
articles.text:
Long-term investors who follow one simple piece of advice have tended to benefit from it: as the market twists and turns, do nothing other than staying the course. But the S&P 500 of today, and the bull market of the past decade, are unique in some ways, led by a concentration at the top in a handful of tech stocks that has few historical precedents.
One "something" that investors have been advised by experts to consider is a move into equal-weight S&P 500 funds to mitigate the risk of having such a high level of exposure to one trade. Well, that didn't exactly work out the way it was supposed to in 2026.
What did investors who adopted the equal-weight approach get? To date, another year trailing the standard market-weight S&P 500 in performance. September was the most brutal month of all for equal weight, capping its longest multi-week losing streak since 2022, with the index falling more than 4%.
To be clear, investors aren't losing money going with equal weight, but they have been making less than investors who stuck with the standard S&P 500.
In recent weeks, the gains made by the index have been highly concentrated, with the S&P 500 hitting new highs even as more of the 500 stocks that comprise the benchmark hit new lows than highs individually. Market breadth, the jargon for how many stocks across the index are contributing to gains, has fallen to its lowest level since the dotcom bubble, according to a recent Goldman Sachs analysis. Meanwhile, going back to the start of 2024, a recent analysis from The Kobeissi Letter finds that a basket of 42 AI stocks generated 67% of the S&P 500's price return.
An analysis this week from DataTrek Research noted that the equal weight S&P 500 has "consistently lagged the market cap weighted version of the index over any given 1-year holding period for almost four years. Moreover, the gap is both larger and has run longer than any point in the last +20 years."
But that has left the market cap-weighted S&P "dramatically overweight," the tech sector, it wrote, and it means equal weight is still at least a "partial substitute" to deal with the risk.
The technology concentration in the S&P 500 isn't going away. Tech stocks now represent about 16% of the equal-weight S&P 500 versus still nearly 40% in the standard index. And now it is tech stocks suddenly looking like the market's shakiest members again, maybe not entirely unrelated to the recent run.
Don't throw equal-weight investing concept out
Equal-weight does still offer a potential response, but the correct way to think about it might be to remove any thought of it being an either/or choice.
"The answer is mostly don't just own an equally weighted ETF," said Todd Rosenbluth, head of research & editorial at TMX VettaFi.
Rather, he says to combine the cap-weighted ETFs and equal-weight options within a portfolio. That means on the market-weight side, allocating to ETFs such as Vanguard's VOO or State Street Investment Management's SPYM — which has become a massive winner this year thanks to its ultra-low expense ratio, undercutting iShares' IVV, and seeing its assets balloon by over $50 billion after becoming the default Trump Account investment.
On the equal-weight side, it can still mean allocating to an ETF like Invesco's equal-weight S&P 500 fund, RSP, which holds the same amount of each of the 500 stocks, though weights can shift between quarterly rebalancing periods. Or, Rosenbluth says, investors can adopt the equal-weight approach at the sector level, using an ETF like the ALPS Equal Weight Sector ETF, EQL, which can serve the same purpose of reducing market concentration in technology stocks.
He says the recent period of underperformance for equal weight is no reason to throw out the concept. In fact, as tech stocks sputter again, it's a moment to reconsider how to employ the concept.
"The recent strength in the cap-weighted ETFs is a further sign of investors putting too few eggs in one basket. If you are a long-term investor who worries the market is being driven by a few stocks, you have alternatives to consider," he said.
Albeit a ridiculously short time frame, over the past five days equal-weight has outperformed again, with defensive sectors like consumer staples leading the market, up nearly 5% this week for its biggest surge since February.
Some experts dismiss the equal-weight mantra and say that if an investor wants to enact a strategy reflecting this approach, just invest in a mid-cap fund in addition to a core S&P 500 holding. Rosenbluth says investors can attempt to balance out the top-heavy S&P 500 through the addition of mid-cap funds, with iShares' core mid-cap portfolio IJH one example.
"They provide exposure to a different set of companies with a mix of growth and stability traits. But these are not large-cap companies. So you are adding different companies to your portfolio for potential diversification benefits," he added.
Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, says investors do need to have their eyes wide open in a market where Nvidia is larger than the entire consumer discretionary sector of the S&P 500. To him, the message to take away is "all about surrounding the core of a portfolio with 'low Tech, low correlation' alternatives."
He says considering an actively managed approach to the "SMID-cap" segment of the market, stocks bridging the gap between small-cap and mid-cap, is a way to manage risk going forward. Or at a minimum, he adds, split an allocation between passive SMID and active SMID.
But Sohn adds that diversifying away from the S&P 500 risk in this environment can also mean thinking about sectors such as natural resources and energy, from metals & mining names to underlying commodities. "Real assets are a diversifier in this environment," he said.
And in fixed income, while recent days have seen bond yields ease off, leading some experts to suggest the worst of the yield surge may be over (though the reasons for that could be tied to a more skeptical outlook on the economy and stock market), Sohn recommends sticking with high-quality, short-duration investment grade fixed income.
Sohn says there are moments in time when equal-weight S&P works, but that's been more of an "easy button" to press in the past, and it is not equal to the task of trying to surround the AI-heavy core of portfolios now.
DataTrek's research shows that the equal weight S&P flipped from outperforming the market cap-weighted index in the decade of 2004-2014 (by 3.2 points on average) to underperforming since 2015 (average of -2.8 points). The global financial crisis and the equal-weight index's underweight in financials helped a lot.
But since the start of this decade, it has only outperformed in 2021, during the height of the speculative stock bubble, and in 2022, when tech stocks took a particular pummeling relative to the rest of the market.
"From mid-2023 to the present, equal weight has consistently underperformed over almost any given 1-year holding period, its longest rough stretch since at least 2004," DataTrek wrote in its analysis.
What is an investor to conclude?
DataTrek says that is up to the investor. You can decide it is "no longer a valid investment approach in a world that concentrates incremental profitability and therefore equity value in a relative handful of largely AI-related businesses."
Or, "that the market has overestimated the value of the world's largest Tech companies, and a reckoning is nigh. The 2008 – 2018 experience lends credence to the second argument. Tech's long history of structural outperformance, driven by continual reinvention and disruptive innovation, supports the former."
Ultimately, DataTrek says investors are lucky to have ETFs to enact both approaches. "We do not see the two versions as competitors, but rather useful partners in portfolio construction," it wrote.

articles.title: Morgan Stanley says quantum computing could be a $100 billion market one day. Here’s its top stock to play the trend
articles.text: Morgan Stanley says quantum computing could become a market worth more than $100 billion annually by 2040. The bank named Quantinuum its top stock pick to capitalize on the opportunity. The investment bank upgraded Quantinuum to overweight from equal-weight, with a $62 price target implying roughly 88% upside from Wednesday's close. Morgan Stanley built its proprietary framework to judge each company on what it has demonstrated across four main areas: technical progress, execution, manufacturability and broader indicators of progress. The bank gave more weight to technology because that's where it found the strongest evidence and clearest differences between the companies. "Quantinuum stands out on technology and execution: it is furthest along among the pure plays and has the strongest execution record, yet the market assigns it the lowest multiple [on] our 2030 revenue in the group," analyst Joseph Moore wrote in a Thursday note. QNT YTD mountain Quantinuum shares in 2026 However, Moore also warns that different hardware approaches make companies hard to compare, and revenue is still too small to separate them. The quantum computing market could grow to more than $100 billion by 20240 from roughly $10 billion in 2030 if "fault toleration machines reach broad commercial adoption", according to the analyst. "No company has built one yet, and current revenue tells investors little about where these businesses end up," Moore wrote. "Company roadmaps converge on early fault-tolerant systems in 2029-30, so we judge the stocks on how credibly each is progressing toward that window." Morgan Stanley expects the Colorado-based company's revenue to soar to $2 billion in 2030 from approximately $270 million in 2028. The bank's analyst identified 2027 as a critical year for the industry, with Quantinuum's next-generation Sol system serving as "the next most important hardware milestone."

articles.title: How to weather the current AI stock storm that we were all dreading
articles.text: We are at a moment that we who own tech have all dreaded. That moment when there may not be as much money out there as we thought we needed to continue the build-out of the fourth industrial revolution that we believe in so passionately. The data center, as central to this revolution as the rails were to the industrial revolution, has to be able to continue to grow. It can't if there isn't enough money. Right now, with the data center stocks cascading and money moving like mad to the drugs and food stocks, there is panic, and that panic includes some of our positions. This is why I am so glad we are having our October Monthly Meeting now, right in the wake of artificial intelligence kingpin Anthropic's earnings announcement, one that fell short of expectations, even as I would point out that a $100 billion annualized run-rate is hardly disappointing. We might even see profitability from this amazing company. So hope should not be lost. The boom we wanted to last forever may be pausing or ending. We think it's the former, because the artificial intelligence revolution is the biggest force i have seen in my 45 years of investing. There will be bumps, fits, starts, but that's par for the course. We never thought, or said, it would all be done in fair weather. It's foul weather out there right now, with our semiconductor and data center component stocks trading down in panic fashion. But we have faith that the sun will come out again. Many money managers have been waiting for the build-out to run its course, or actually thought it was phony, and they think with these somewhat weaker Anthropic numbers and the debt problems of thinly capitalized companies like CoreWeave , the future is collapsing. One person, by the way, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia , came out Thursday and said that CoreWeave is fine, doesn't need help — and, in fact, the company's cost of capital is actually decreasing because Nvidia chips more than hold their value. That statement actually turned the entire tech market around — at least for Thursday. Still, the possibility of a political nightmare, a wave of states voting no to new data centers in the midterm election, makes it all even uglier. Maybe the midterms further quash the data center build-out. And then, the next day after the election, will President Donald Trump make good on his decision to restart the war against Iran — and perhaps expand it to the Houthis. It's all on the table. At the same time, a new Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh , has come in, and he's not messing around. Warsh will bring inflation down to the central bank's 2% target after years and years above that level. But he will do so by the blunt instrument of raising interest rates. To get the inflation rate down to 2%, Warsh might have to take short-term rates to 5.5% or even 6%. The current range for short-term policy rates is 3.75% to 4% following the Fed hiking last month for the first time in three years. The market sees at least one more rate increase by year-end. The longer end, which the Fed does not control, could go to 5.5% to 7% or 8%. We are not set up for that. Given the flight to quality rising from the data center woes, we don't need to at this point because our diversification strategy is playing out fabulously. Still, we aren't so confident that rates will be this low a month from now — not with the hot consumer price index on Wednesday and hot producer price index and retail sales numbers on Thursday and not with $100-per-barrel oil that won't seem to go away. So, what does it mean for us, and for you? Rather suddenly, if you own technology stocks, you are fighting what we used to call the tape, the ticker tape on which quotes used to appear. This tape wants to go lower. If we are buying stocks now, especially tech stocks, we are also fighting the Fed, which is now raising rates, never a good situation for stock owners. Those of you old enough to remember market legend Marty Zweig, a regular on "Wall Street Week with Louis Rukeyser," know that he was by far the most practical and historical figure in the business. He had simple rules, but ones that have to be obeyed or you will lose a lot of money. I remember them like it is 1981 all over again. His two most important: Don't fight the Fed and don't fight the tape. Club members, even with 12% of our funds in cash, much higher than usual, and even with big sales like that of Corning that we talked about at length when we met last month, we find ourselves fighting both the Fed and the tape with many of our positions. That makes me uncomfortable. You won't find us putting on a lot of new stock without taking some off, as we have been doing consistently for some time now. Before the meeting , we took profits in a rallying stock we still really like, Cardinal Health , and bought additional shares of Bank of New York , which had great earnings Thursday. As I said on Wednesday night's "Mad Money," it will not be an easy moment for us. We know that there are some positives out there that could make it so we will be fully embracing the tape, not fighting it. If the president solves the war with Iran — which I don't think will happen anytime soon — we will wish we could borrow money and be 120% long all sorts of stocks. That's how explosive the bull will be. If oil plummets to $40, where I think it will go when the war ends because the world is wildly overproducing, you will no longer be fighting the Fed. The Fed will be on your side, and we will be done with rate hikes. So we are being kept up at night because we own too much tech if the war doesn't end and data center funding dwindles, especially if the midterm election produces multiple data center bans. And, we are being kept up at night because we might not own enough tech because there are no important data center bans and the war ends sooner than the cognoscenti expect. Most of all, we want to be in nothing but the highest quality stocks with the best balance sheets so we can ride this one through. We have made a point of avoiding the speculative stocks, and we have high-graded this portfolio as much as we could. That will, ultimately, get us through even this treacherous moment. articles.text:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple, the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.
Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.
The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture. As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.
Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.
Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.
Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.
Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."
Ternus responded, "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.
The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.
"We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.
Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.
Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.
Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.
Common ground on open source
The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models, it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang, who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.
While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.
"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.
Their leaders have also traded harsh words.
Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.
Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.
Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.
And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.
Apple's multiple partners
Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.
In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration "dramatically underperformed" and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.
Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google, to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.
Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.
Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.
Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer, with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.
Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.
"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."
WATCH: Apple makes its biggest smart-home push yet under CEO John Ternus.

articles.title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
articles.text:
CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
'Self-fulfilling prophecy'
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

articles.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Salesforce, Rocket Lab, Kimberly-Clark & more
articles.text:
Market Insider
Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Salesforce, Rocket Lab, Kimberly-Clark & more 
Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Semiconductors — Chipmakers fell on Thursday, dragging the tech sector lower on the day. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) is heading for its eighth losing day, down 2% in the session. Shares of Nvidia lost nearly 2%, while shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Marvell Technology fell more than 3%. Software makers — Software companies were a bright spot within the tech sector, with the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) adding about 1%. Shares of Salesforce gained almost 4%, while shares of Adobe rose more than 3%. Oracle 's stock climbed 2%. Consumer staples — Shares of consumer staples companies rose as investors fled the tech sector for relative safety. Campbell's stock added about 5%, and shares of General Mills and Conagra Brands gained more than 3% each. FMC Corp — Shares tanked 32% after the chemical manufacturing company slashed its guidance for the third quarter. The company now sees revenue in a range between $65 million and $125 million, sharply below the FactSet consensus estimate of $868.5 million. "Q3 demand was weaker than we expected, driven by challenging market conditions and elevated levels of higher-priced FMC products held in inventory by certain channel customers, which are limiting product movement and replenishment demand," said CEO Pierre Brondeau in a statement . Intuit — Shares added 6% after the company behind TurboTax and QuickBooks software announced that it will acquire Sequence , a revenue management platform. Kimberly-Clark — The maker of Huggies diapers saw its stock gain about 4% after it issued preliminary third-quarter results that topped Wall Street's estimates. The company earned $1.70 per share, excluding certain items, on revenue of $4.13 billion. That compares to the FactSet consensus call for $1.58 per share and $4.09 billion. Berkshire Hathaway — Shares ticked up 0.4% and headed for an 11th consecutive winning day. On Wednesday, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons announced that Berkshire made a $330 million investment into the company. That's in addition to Berkshire's $600 million infusion into the company in July when Bending Spoons debuted on the Nasdaq. The RealReal — Shares rose 11% after the online marketplace for designer clothes announcrd that it has obtained a $150 million term loan as well as a $25 million senior secured revolving credit facility. The RealReal will use the proceeds to refinance its 2029 senior secured notes. Marsh & McLennan — The insurer saw shares jump 5% on the back of top- and bottom-line beats for the third quarter. Marsh reported adjusted earnings of $2.03 per share on revenue of $6.86 billion, compared with the FactSet consensus of $1.97 per share and $6.64 billion. The advance led the SPDR Insurance ETF (KIE) 1% higher on the day. CoreWeave — Shares of the cloud infrastructure technology company fell for a second day, losing 2% on Thursday as investors worry that CoreWeave, along with other technology companies, are borrowing too much for an artificial intelligence build-out. Artificial Intelligence infrastructure plays Nebius Group and Iren also slid 5% and nearly 8%, respectively. Shares of Dell Technologies lost 8%, and shares of data storage company Everpure fell 6%. Rocket Lab — The space company's stock dropped 11% after it delayed the launch of its Neutron rocket to 2027. SK Hynix — Shares of the South Korea-based company slid 2% as investors are concerned over funding the artificial intelligence build-out. The drop also follows a 7.6% drop in the South Korean Kospi index overnight. Penske Automotive — Shares popped 8% after the transportation company said it would be taken private by Motown Acquisition Corp., an entity owned by Penske Corp. and Mitsui, for $212 per share in cash. The deal represents a nearly 9% premium to Wednesday's closing price of $194.79 per share. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Walmart — Shares of the retailer popped more than 2% after Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to buy from hold, citing a positive outlook for 2027. The bank expects incremental margins to improve and noted current inflation levels could help the company attract consumers. Crocs — The footwear company's stock rose 6% after Barclays upgraded Crocs to overweight from equal weight. Analyst Adrienne Yih cited the company's progress on product innovation and category expansion and its international business growth as factors for the upgrade. — CNBC's Fred Imbert, Tom Rotunno and Nick Wells contributed reporting

articles.title: International Energy Agency to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible
articles.text:
International Energy Agency members have agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel "as soon as possible" as fuel prices surge globally, the group said in a statement Thursday.
President Donald Trump said earlier this month that Europe had agreed to deploy a "massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil." The release detailed by the IEA on Thursday is equivalent to less than one day of global diesel demand or slightly more than five days of U.S. consumption.
The IEA did not specify a timeline for the release in its Thursday statement. The Group of Seven nations led by France said on Oct. 2 that they would deploy substantial diesel stocks over 20 days. If that is the IEA's timeline, its members would supply about 1 million barrels each day for almost three weeks.
Diesel futures are trading more than 1% lower Thursday at $4.86.
The IEA, headquartered in Paris, has more than 30 member states, including the U.S. and key European and Asian allies. The agency, created in 1974 in the wake of the Arab oil embargo, is tasked with maintaining energy security by deploying oil stockpiles in response to crises like the wars in the Middle East and Eastern Europe.
The Trump administration has pushed Europe to release diesel inventories as prices in the U.S. surged to record highs in September. The retail price of diesel stood at an average $6.32 per gallon Thursday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA.
Trump is facing political pressure to address fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. The president struck a diesel deal with Russia last week that analysts have said will do little to reduce prices.
The G7 nations, led by France, announced earlier this month that they would deploy stocks through the IEA in response to the diesel crisis but did not give specific quantities.
The IEA release does "not solve the basic problem which is how to increase production at refineries which are damaged in the Middle East or Russia, and operating at capacity in the USA," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Prices have surged as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries and Iran and its Houthi allies have attacked energy facilities around the Persian Gulf.
IEA members agreed in March to deploy 400 million barrels of oil in response to the global supply disruption triggered by the Iran war. They have since agreed to release the remaining 100 million barrels pledged in March "in a timely manner consistent with national circumstances," the group said Thursday.
IEA's governing board said 330 million barrels have been released so far. Some members have deployed more than they originally pledged so the total release will exceed the 400 million barrels agreed in March.

articles.title: JetBlue’s new domestic first class, BlueFirst, is now on sale
articles.text:
JetBlue's new domestic first class, BlueFirst, is now available for booking on flights across more than 30 routes, the airline said Thursday.
This option will be available on domestic flights that are not currently served by the airline's lie-flat Mint business class, which it offers on longer flights. It's part of an overhaul of the carrier's fare options, which will include basic options that don't come with things like seat assignments, a standard option, and a "flex" option, which is refundable and more easily changed.
The new first-class section comes as JetBlue seeks to return to steady profitability by growing its higher-priced offerings amid strong demand for more expensive and roomier seats.
The first flight with BlueFirst seats will be on Dec. 8, between Boston and Fort Lauderdale, Florida, followed by routes between Fort Lauderdale and New York's LaGuardia Airport, with additional flights being rolled out in the following weeks and months.
JetBlue is offering some introductory fares for BlueFirst seats for select flights, including a $299 flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, a $249 option from New York to Fort Lauderdale and a $299 option from New York to Liberia, Costa Rica.
The first-class tickets will offer seats that recline up to 5 inches and have up to 7 inches more legroom than Main seats, JetBlue said. Other perks include Bluetooth-connected seatback screens, food and beverage options, Group 1 boarding and expedited security.
Within the BlueFirst class, there are three tiered fare options:
- BlueFirst Base, a lower-cost option, includes one checked bag, priority check-in and security, and Group 1 boarding. Seat selection is free within 24 hours of departure, but there are fees for changes and cancellations.
- BlueFirst includes two checked bags, free seat selection, and no change or cancellation fees.
- BlueFirst Flex has the same perks as BlueFirst and additionally offers refunds if you cancel your flight ahead of the departure, with no fees for same-day switches or standby.
"We designed BlueFirst to deliver a more accessible first-class experience that combines the thoughtful hospitality and service customers expect from JetBlue with exceptional value and comfort. We're excited that customers can now start making BlueFirst part of their travel plans," JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty said in a news release.

articles.title: What's behind the sell-off in AI neocloud stocks like CoreWeave and Nebius
articles.text: CoreWeave equity and debt are trying to find their footing after a tweet-fueled sell-off on Wednesday that saw shares slump 15%. On Thursday, the stock is continuing to slide, off about 3%, while the yield on CoreWeave's 2032 bond is up to 15.77% and 5-year credit default swaps, a sort of insurance on debt, are up to a spread of 1140 basis points, or 11.4% per year. CRWV 1M mountain CoreWeave shares in the past month Beyond general pressure stemming from concerns about the AI borrowing binge, tightening credit conditions and rising inflation , coupled with Wednesday's social media posts , multiple tech investors that CNBC spoke to were mostly at a loss for a specific rationale for the sell-off in what are called neocloud stocks. Neoclouds are specialized computing providers built for artificial intelligence and machine learning. Freak out One person said they were "freaked out" by the slump in their stock and bond prices. However, a Wednesday analysis from research firm Gartner may point to the answer: a longer time horizon for AI capital returns driving eventual consolidation in the neocloud space. "By 2030, Gartner predicts that cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model will force over 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations," the analysis said. Underpinning this analysis is growing conviction among investors that AI is going to take longer than initially forecast to generate the returns needed to justify the required investment. "What if that payoff does not arrive with the speed that the consensus was expecting? What if that payoff arrives slower?" Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok said on CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Thursday. Weak link Assuming a longer time horizon is required for returns on AI capital, the neocloud sector could be the weak link in the AI value chain, especially because its equipment wears out and needs to be replaced so often. AI-specific "infrastructure-as-a-service" spending is forecast to grow to $174 billion in 2030 from $66 billion in 2027 – a tiny fraction of the $3.6 trillion that data center owners as a whole are expected to spend, according to Gartner. That $3.6 trillion is itself less than half of of the $8.5 trillion in revenue required to cover capex and debt service to achieve a 12% return. Due to all the debt on CoreWeave's balance sheet – resulting in a forward debt-to-equity ratio of 667-to-1, according to FactSet – the company is regarded by many investors as a bellwether for the entire neocloud sector. Its leverage will allow it to do very well if its business model proves to be viable, and it could be the first to tank if not. "CoreWeave is the canary in the coal mine in the neocloud business," Paul Meeks, head of tech research at Freedom Capital Markets, said. Frontier model Anthropic also reported third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, or 45%. That's a significant step down in revenue growth from earlier in the year at 140%. Moving together The neoclouds are moving in tandem Thursday, with Nebius down about 5% and IREN falling almost 9% in late morning trading. Those declines suggest it's the neocloud business model, as opposed to the capital structures of the specific companies in the sector, that investors are scrutinizing. "Look at a comparable company like Nebius," said Gil Luria, head of tech research at DA Davidson. "They literally sell the same thing to the same companies and have almost no financial leverage." So-called AI colos – short for "colocation" firms – are also down Thursday. This may further support the idea that it's a broader issue regarding return on invested capital for similar AI infrastructure providers that's pressuring CoreWeave -- or it could illustrate the contagious nature of problems in the sector. AI colos are companies like Applied Digital , Hut 8 , TeraWulf and Cipher Digital that can own their own servers, power and other hardware while leasing out space in third-party data centers. Some started out as cryptocurrency miners. "Sometimes the AI colos are actually landlords of the neoclouds, and so you would assume that if CoreWeave got in trouble, it would take down the entire group," Meeks said. Applied Digital is off 5.5% Thursday, Hut 8 is lower by 8.4%, Terawulf by nearly 3% and Ciper Digital is pulling back another 6%.

articles.title: Josh Brown says this is his AI roller coaster stock
articles.text: (This is The Best Stocks in the Market , brought to you by Josh Brown and Sean Russo of Ritholtz Wealth Management.) Josh — The Ferrari World theme park opened its doors in Abu Dhabi in November 2010. The centerpiece of the park is Formula Rossa, which Guinness verified this spring as the fastest roller coaster launch ride on planet Earth. It employs a hydraulic launcher similar to the one used to catapult fighter jets off the top of an aircraft carrier. Your body is sent into a 240 km per hour (about 149 mph) rush in under 5 seconds when the ride takes off, and it hits 100 km per hour within the opening 2 seconds. At that speed, even ordinary dust in the air hits the skin like a bullet. Riders are made to wear eye goggles and leave anything they're carrying behind before boarding the train, which is shaped like an actual F1 car. The ride lasts about a minute, but that sounds like plenty of time to me. Riding an AI software stock like Palantir (PLTR) this year is the closest you'll get to the Formula Rossa experience without traveling to Yas Island. It has a beta of 1.6, meaning the shares move 60% more than the stock market, which works in both directions. But even beta understates how extreme the ride has been. Over the last five years the annualized standard deviation is 71%, several times what the broader market runs. The five-year max drawdown is 85%, and yet the stock is now just a few percentage points away from a record high. I point this out to warn you that if roller coasters aren't your thing, you may want to sit this one out. Not everybody getting off the ride, stumbling to see their picture on the wall, agrees that the thrills were worth the chills. We're going to tell you the story and show you the charts regardless. Palantir has just hit our list again as of last week and we haven't covered it yet in this column. Sean has the fundamentals below. I'll be back with the technicals and where we'd be wrong. Best Stock Spotlight: Palantir Technologies, Inc. (PLTR) Sean — Palantir was one of the original holdings when we launched Porterhouse, our in-house momentum strategy, in January. The model sold it at our April rebalance and it has not made its way back. However, just last week it popped up on our Best Stocks list, so we thought it would be a fun spotlight. PLTR closed at a record $207.18 last November, then fell 48% to a June low near $107 as all of software sold off. It then nearly doubled to a new record close of $209.05 on Oct. 9. As of Wednesday's close, it's up 13% YTD and up 55% over the last three months. Palantir builds software that lets governments and large companies run their operations on their own data and AI models. It started with U.S. defense and intelligence agencies and today the company is quickly expanding its commercial business. Private corporations have become the fastest-growing business for PLTR. Let's dive in. The business never slowed down during the "SaaSpocalypse." Revenue growth has accelerated for nine straight quarters, from 27% in Q2 2024 to 93% in Q2 2026, on $1.94B of revenue. U.S. commercial grew 149% and U.S. government grew 90%. Net dollar retention hit 157%, which means existing customers are spending 57% more than a year ago. Net income topped $1B in a quarter for the first time. That combination of growth and margin shows up in the oft-talked-about "Rule of 40," which adds revenue growth to profit margin. Anything above 40 is considered a healthy software company. Palantir's score was 155 in Q2, using its 62% adjusted operating margin, and it was the 12th straight quarter that score improved. Microsoft scores about 66, and CrowdStrike, at a similar revenue size, scores about 45. The only large companies ahead of PLTR are Micron (427), SK Hynix (333), Samsung (182). Management has raised 2026 revenue guidance at every print this year. It went from $7.19B (61% growth) in February to $8.15B (82% growth) in August. Q3 guidance implies 83% growth, and the company reports on November 2. The backlog backs that up - total remaining deal value is $13.1 billion, up 83%. In September, Palantir expanded its partnership with Nvidia to pair Nvidia's open models with Palantir's platform, which lets customers run AI on their own data and keep the models they train. Nvidia is using that setup for its own supply chains. None of this is cheap. Investors are paying up for growth. At a $483B market cap, Palantir trades at 59x this year's revenue guidance and about 78x consensus 2027 earnings. The stock is back where it was last November, but quarterly revenue is 64% higher than it was then. This makes it a cheaper stock today than it was the last time it hit an all-time high. Risk management Josh — Palantir gapped out of a base on Aug. 4, opening near $145 after closing in the mid-120s the session before. The stock had spent most of 2026 under its 200-day and bottomed in the low $100s in late June. This is a breakaway gap on the heaviest volume of the year, and the Q2 report Sean described above is the reason. Institutions paid up and weren't willing to wait. The gap has never been filled, and the September pullback found buyers at $166 twice, nowhere near it. The stock cleared the $195 ceiling from late September on Oct. 8, then took out last November's record the next day and ran to a high near $213 on Monday. Wednesday's 4% drop left it at $201, and it's opening soft this morning at around $195. Meanwhile, we have the 50-day rising at $181 and the 200-day at $153. Monday's high is the ceiling to clear. RSI stayed elevated for weeks after the August gap and the stock held. September then flushed it into the low 40s on the pullback to $166, a full reset that cleared the way for this second leg. The Oct. 9 push to the record took RSI back into the low 70s. With RSI at 63 after Wednesday's drop, momentum has cooled by nearly ten points in a single session. One red day from a record high is a small dent next to that September flush, and the reading leaves room for another run at Monday's high without starting from a stretched level. Traders can't use $195 here. The stock is opening right on top of it, so it's not a stop, it's the battle. Traders can use $185 as their stop, a 5% drop from here. That's the floor of the late September and early October consolidation, where buyers held the stock between $185 and $187 for two weeks before it broke out. A close below it puts the stock back inside that range and tells you the breakout didn't take. If you're wrong, you'll know fast, and it won't cost you much to find out. Let the closing print decide, not the intraday noise. Investors can anchor to $166, where both September lows came in. The gap near $145 and the 200-day at $153 sit well below that, which makes $166 the line for patient holders. A weekly close below it and the sequence of higher lows since the gap is broken. Put your goggles on if you're playing. You have my permission to skip and get in the churro line instead. articles.title: Economists: Hot PPI shows Fed's work is not done
articles.text:
Wall Street estimates for the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation indicator now expect an acceleration from the level that prompted the central bank to hike rates last month.
The estimates come after a hotter-than-expected producer price index came in at 1.3% Thursday, the biggest monthly gain since March 2022 and more than double the 0.6% consensus.
That drove the year-over-year increase to 6.3%, the biggest jump since December 2022. The increase was paced by a 20% rise in gasoline prices. But taking out food, energy and trade services, prices still rose a healthy 0.5%, indicating that inflation was broader than just energy.
Seven Wall Street estimates gathered by CNBC show core personal consumption expenditures inflation for September, which will be published later this month, is forecast to rise 0.32%, up from 0.25% in August. Wall Street economists use the consumer price index, released Wednesday, and the PPI to estimate the PCE.
"We see real risks the Fed will deliver another rate hike in two weeks' time even as recent Fedspeak tempered expectations for back-to-back increases,'' wrote Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.
Several Fed officials have argued that the Fed does not need to hurry to hike rates, though they have suggested more rate hikes are needed. As a result, Fed futures on Thursday showed just a 29% probability of a hike at the Fed meeting at the end of this month, but a 91% probability of at least one hike by December.
A 0.32% increase in PCE would boost the year-over-year core inflation rate to 3.1%, up from 3.01% in August. Estimates ranged from a high of 0.35% from Barclays to a low of 0.29% from Oxford Economics.
"The picture is not benign with inflation elevated and intensifying," wrote Alex Pelle, senior U.S. economist at Mizuho Securities. "On the economic data alone, there is little reason for the Fed to hesitate to continue moving the policy rate higher."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has suggested one litmus test for not hiking is confidence that inflation will return in a timely manner to the Fed's 2% target. Both headline and core PCE inflation have been above target since 2021. They have inched steadily higher since tariffs were introduced in April 2025. The gains have accelerated since the beginning of the Iran war.
The Fed prefers the PCE because, compared to the CPI, it believes it more closely resembles how Americans actually spend their money and changes its weightings when consumers change their spending patterns.

articles.title: Banks with Jeffrey Epstein ties eyed by Democrats Warren and Garcia
articles.text:
Financial institutions and bank executives that may have aided the late financier Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking operation are in the sights of a bipartisan group of lawmakers.
Legislation introduced Thursday — and led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — would require financial regulators to produce records related to Epstein, compel those regulators to investigate banks and executives with ties to the deceased convicted sex offender, and require industry bans and civil penalties for those found to have aided him.
"I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump's financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein's horrific crimes," Warren, who leads the Senate banking committee's Democrats, said in a statement. "Since they have failed to act, Congress must. The bipartisan Epstein Wall Street Records Act will ensure overdue accountability for the wealthy and well-connected on Wall Street who put profits over people."
The legislation is co-led in the House by Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill. Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., signed on to the Senate version. The House version has 17 Democratic co-sponsors.
The proposal would apply to the Federal Reserve, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Spokespeople for the Federal Reserve and the OCC declined to comment. Spokespeople for the other regulators did not respond to requests for comment.
Since the start of Trump's second term, Democrats and a small group of Republicans have pressed the president to release records related to Epstein and to investigate the individuals and businesses associated with him.
Warren has sought answers from Barclays, Goldman Sachs, and JP Morgan Chase on their connections to Epstein. And Wyden, in his capacity as the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, released an investigation in August that found "significant evidence that JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, and Bank of America violated federal anti-money laundering laws by failing to screen and report Epstein's suspicious financial transactions in a timely manner."
Barclays, Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan Chase all declined to comment on Thursday.
The fallout from the Epstein files has been politically perilous for Republicans, who largely opposed an effort, led by Massie and Khanna, to force a vote to release the documents. After Trump belatedly signaled his support for the legislation, the Epstein Files Transparency Act passed both chambers of Congress with near unanimity and was signed into law in November 2025. The legislation was meant to force the Department of Justice to release its records related to Epstein.
But ahead of November's midterm election, Democrats in recent weeks have ramped up campaign ads hitting their GOP opponents for past opposition to releasing the Epstein files. And those who advocated for public disclosure of the files have continued to push for accountability in Washington and on Wall Street.
"The Epstein Files Transparency Act forced the Attorney General to release DOJ, FBI, and U.S. Attorney's Offices' files. This bill does the same for bank regulators. Justice for the survivors means following the money," Massie, who had a falling out with Trump over his effort to release the Epstein files, said in a statement.

articles.title: We're trimming a rallying defensive stock and buying another on a muted earnings move
articles.text: We're making two trades ahead of Thursday's Monthly Meeting livestream , starting at noon ET. Selling 50 shares of Cardinal Health at roughly $251 each; reducing our CAH stake in Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust to 425 shares and decreasing its weighting in the portfolio to 2.75% from 3% Buying 75 shares of Bank of New York at roughly $138; increasing our BNY position in the Trust to 675 shares and increasing its weighting to 2.35% from 2.1%. A major rotation is happening in the market on Thursday, with selling in AI and data center buildout winners and buying into defensive groups like healthcare and consumer staples that don't need a hot economy to hit their earnings targets. We're taking advantage of this move into healthcare to lock in profits in Cardinal Health, which is up more than 5% this week and on pace to close at a new record high. With shares at a high, we're downgrading the stock to our hold-equivalent 2 rating . CAH YTD mountain Cardinal Health YTD We picked at Cardinal Health over the past few months, buying 50 shares around $230 in August and another 50 shares in September in the low $230s after a big pullback. What got the stock moving back up again was news that it extended its distribution agreement with CVS Health . We called the update a clearing event , and this rally above $250 has come even faster than we expected. With the market now rushing to buy stocks with limited economic and data center exposure, we'll take the other side of that trade and lock in nice-sized profits on this position. From this sale, we will realize a gain of about 9% on stock purchased in March 2026. We still like Cardinal Health very much. We're using the proceeds from the Cardinal Health trim to pick up more shares of Bank of New York. The financial services company reported a better-than-expected quarter Thursday: Revenue of $5.7 billion and earnings per share (EPS) of $2.37 versus estimates of $5.5 billion and $2.27, respectively, according to LSEG. The bank beat Street expectations on fee-based revenue and net interest income (NII). While costs were a little higher than expected, the beat on revenue more than made up for the expense miss. BNY YTD mountain Bank of New York YTD BNY's earnings came one day after the trust bank State Street reported disappointing results, which took down the group. But BNY's numbers look much cleaner and its 29% Return on Tangible Common Equity (RTOCE) is proof. We thought BNY's earnings looked good enough for a positive response Thursday, especially given how far the stock has pulled back in the past six weeks. With shares right around the flat line, we're taking this opportunity to scale deeper into the new position. Members, check your texts and email inboxes after our noon ET Monthly Meeting for our full BNY earnings analysis. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long CAH, BNY. articles.title: TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
articles.text:
As Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s record quarter makes clear, demand from chipmakers shows no sign of slowing down. In fact, TSMC can't manufacture quickly enough.
The artificial intelligence boom has created unending need for space on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, and it could put a chokehold on the entire industry's ability to scale. Last year, TSMC said it had the capacity to make more than 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. But customers want more.
"The competition is extremely fierce," said Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities. "It's a game of who can get the most leverage and supply."
TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, the graphics processors and central processors from Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom that are necessary for running AI workloads. Now a growing number of tech firms – Apple, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI – also rely on TSMC to make custom in-house AI accelerators.
TSMC North American CEO Sajiv Dalal told CNBC he gets at least 10 calls a day about wafer capacity. TSMC posted record profit for a sixth straight quarter on Thursday and expects fourth-quarter revenue to be 58% higher than a year earlier, driven by strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies.
If compute demand continues to grow at the current rate over the next 12 to 18 months, Klein said capacity constraints at TSMC could threaten some of the industry's massive infrastructure investments and the "aggressive revenue growth targets" from the AI companies. U.S. hyperscalers are projecting well over $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, and analysts expect that figure to jump in 2027.
AI ambitions are also threatened by a global shortage of memory chips. The logic chips that TSMC manufactures are more complex and expensive to produce. That means GPU and CPU leaders like Nvidia and AMD work out lengthy contracts and bespoke deals with TSMC behind closed doors years in advance. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su have both visited Taiwan multiple times this year.
Sid Sheth, CEO of AI chip startup D-Matrix, has fostered a relationship with TSMC for more than 20 years, and his company relies on TSMC to manufacture its processors.
For TSMC customers, many roads lead to Kevin Zhang, a senior vice president of the Taiwanese company and a central figure in determining which chipmakers get access to its coveted factory lines.
He's "currently probably the most popular person on the planet," Sheth said in an interview. Sheth said that Jerry Qubain, D-Matrix's vice president of manufacturing, has been visiting TSMC since 1992 and goes to Taiwan three to four times a year.
"This was even before Nvidia was founded," Sheth said. "That's a good example of a person we brought on board because of the relationships he has at TSMC." Qubain joined D-Matrix in 2024. TSMC declined to participate in this story.
Betting on startups
TSMC had 534 customers in 2025. While it doesn't name or rank them, its top 10 customers accounted for 78% of net revenue, with its top two bringing in 19% and 17%, respectively.
That leaves startups competing for capacity against customers with far bigger orders. Sheth said TSMC is "selective," but has an incentive to back promising newcomers.
"They were very supportive of Nvidia and Broadcom when they were very young companies, and now these are their biggest customers today," Sheth said. "They want to see a repeat of that."
TSMC is hustling to bring much more capacity online, with new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona — it's making advanced chips in the U.S. for the first time. In July, TSMC announced it was adding $100 billion and "several more" fabs to the six planned in Arizona, bringing its total commitment to $265 billion. TSMC is also reportedly considering an entirely new fab location in Texas.
All of this will take years to come online. In the meantime, analysts say TSMC is adding tools like ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to existing factories to ramp up capacity. ASML smashed profit expectations in its earnings report Wednesday and said customers are interested in placing orders through 2030.
TSMC isn't the only option. Capacity constraints create an opening for the other two leading advanced chip manufacturers, Samsung and Intel, to win customers.
"People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Dan Hutcheson, an analyst at TechInsights, told CNBC.
That second source might be Intel, the only U.S.-based advanced logic manufacturer. Although its foundry business has been struggling with delays and setbacks for years, Hutcheson says all the big chipmakers are now testing there.
Trade association SEMI expects 102 new chip fabs will come online globally by 2029, including 15 in the U.S. and 78 in Asia. China is the primary growth engine, expected to nearly triple capacity by 2030. In a race to catch up, American fab investments are projected to more than double by 2029.
With an increasing Arizona presence and "extremely fierce" competition for wafer capacity, Klein says TSMC is "one of the best strategically positioned companies on the face of the planet."

articles.title: USPS postmarks can lag mailing dates. What taxpayers and voters should know
articles.text:
U.S. Postal Service postmark practices that were formalized in a December 2025 rule could mean a longer delay between when something is mailed and when it's postmarked — a distinction that matters for tax returns, mail-in ballots and other time-sensitive documents.
The issue may crop up as two deadlines approach: Oct. 15 for taxpayers who received a six-month extension to file their federal income tax returns, and Nov. 3 for voters casting ballots in the midterm elections.
Taxpayers who mail their return can meet Thursday's deadline by taking it to the post office for a manual postmark. But voters casting ballots by mail for the midterms can't necessarily count on the same rule.
That's because while the IRS generally considers a return filed on the day it is postmarked, most states require mail-in ballots to arrive by Election Day, regardless of when they were mailed or postmarked. A postmark shows the date your mail was processed, which may not be the day you mailed the ballot.
Thirty-five states require mailed absentee ballots to be received by election officials on or before Election Day, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan organization that tracks state laws and policies. The other 15 states — along with Washington, Guam, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands — generally allow ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive afterward, usually within a specified number of days.
"State laws govern elections for the most part, and every state has chosen a little bit different way of doing things," said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the NCSL.
About 1.2% of 2024 mail-in ballots rejected
Nearly 48 million voters cast absentee ballots in the 2024 presidential election, representing roughly 30% of the total 158.2 million ballots cast, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. The absentee figure includes mail-in ballots as well as those returned through drop boxes or in person.
About 1.2% of the mail-in ballots cast in 2024 were rejected, according to the commission. Of them, 40.7% were rejected because the signature on the return envelope didn't match the one on file or was incomplete, and 10% were rejected because they lacked any signature. Another 17.8% were rejected because they were not received by the state's deadline.
Those deadlines vary from state to state. In California, for instance, mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive as many as seven days afterward and still be counted, according to NCSL. Colorado, by contrast, requires mail-in ballots to be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day. Some states give military and overseas voters additional time for ballots to arrive after Election Day.
In a June ruling, the Supreme Court upheld states' authority to count mail-in ballots received after Election Day, provided they were cast on time and meet state deadlines.
Mail ballots a week before Election Day
Voters should be aware that, generally, it may take longer than they expect for ballots to reach election offices, and that postmarks may not be applied the day they mail their ballot.
This is because the U.S. Postal Service has been overhauling its operations, which over time has included reduced pickups at many postal locations and increased travel times for mail to reach regional processing centers where postmarks are applied. The upshot is that the agency expects longer delays between when mail is sent and when it is postmarked, according to a Postal Service rule that took effect in December 2025.
In practice, this means some mail doesn't begin moving through the system until at least the day after you mail it, so the postmark isn't applied the day you mailed it. In some cases — i.e., ahead of weekends or holidays — it could take longer for a postmark to be applied, according to the Brookings Institution, a think tank.
However, beginning on Oct. 24, the Postal Service said it plans to use "extraordinary measures" to speed up delivery of mail-in ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 election — such as making additional deliveries to election offices. Starting on Oct. 26, postal workers are also supposed to hand-postmark ballots being delivered directly to local election offices or routed through postal hubs to other election offices, according to a USPS memorandum.
"These things are going above and beyond what the Postal Service does for other pieces of mail," said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, a nonprofit organization for election administrators.
Nevertheless, those actions don't guarantee a voter's ballot will arrive by their state's deadline.
For voters who will mail in their ballot, "try to get it in the mail a week before it's due," Patrick said. "If it's closer to Election Day and they live in a state that allows for a postmark [to establish a deadline is met], they can go into any post office and go up to the counter and ask to have it be hand-postmarked."
Meanwhile, taxpayers who file their return online can avoid the postmark issue altogether. Those who need to mail their return should ask a postal worker for a manual postmark, or send it via certified mail.

articles.title: This used car stock is likely to cruise higher, Bank of America says
articles.text: CarMax can rally as its competitive prices become more apparent to consumers, according to Bank of America. The bank double upgraded the used car stock to buy from underperform. It also raised its price target on shares to $65 from $50, suggesting 30% upside from Wednesday's close. "FTC enforcement of price transparency, combined with KMX's own actions, has made KMX the most price-competitive it has been in years, driving share gains," analyst Alexander Perry said Thursday in a note to clients. "We see a longer tail given increased compliance and better perceived pricing builds repeat customers." KMX YTD mountain KMX year to date This year, the Federal Trade Commission began promoting more price transparency in the used car market. "For years, KMX's low- or no-fee all-in prices were compared vs competitor advertised prices that excluded hidden fees," Perry wrote. "Industry compliance with the FTC's price-transparency push, which began in May, should help KMX take share from dealers forced to advertise higher prices. CarMax's unit comparables were up 13% on a year-over-year basis for the fiscal second quarter, while those of its public peers declined 4% on average over the same period, according to Bank of America. Bank of America's call goes against consensus on Wall Street. Of the 22 analysts covering CarMax, 17 have a hold rating on the stock, while just three have a strong buy on it, LSEG data shows. Shares are up about 29% year to date.

articles.title: Southwest is overhauling its frequent flyer program. Here's what's changing
articles.text:
Goodbye, A-List and A-List Preferred.
Southwest Airlines is scrapping its two-tier loyalty program starting next year and instead rolling out silver, gold and platinum levels that are similar to what other carriers offer, as the once-quirky airline seeks to increase revenue and reward its biggest spenders.
Southwest executives have been overhauling the airline, getting rid of longtime customer perks like two free checked bags and open seating. It's now charging for some of those options, like rivals have been doing for years.
Along with the shift from two to three loyalty levels, the carrier is also changing the names of its tiers. Under the old version, travelers could be classified into A-List or A-List Preferred, which was the higher level.
"If you think about A-List and A-List Preferred, we don't even have [boarding] groups A, B and C anymore," Tony Roach, Southwest chief customer and brand officer, said in an interview. "So it was time to do a refresh to somewhat incorporate all the changes to seating and all these new experiences that we've been adding."
Here's what's changing for the loyalty program:
- A-List and A-List Preferred Rapid Rewards status levels will go away on Jan. 1.
- A-List customers will be shifted to Silver status in the Rapid Rewards program. A-List Preferred members will get Gold status.
- A new Platinum tier will be added for the airline's "most engaged" customers.
Customers can earn 1 Tier Qualifying Point, or TQP, per $1 spent on Southwest co-branded credit cards with Chase. Here are the new status requirements:
- Silver status will require 35,000 TQPs or 25 qualifying flights. Previously, A-List was 35,000 points or 20 flights. For Silver members, the points-earning bonus on flights will go up from 25% to 40%.
- To earn Gold, customers will have to reach 65,000 TQPs, down from 70,000 points for A-List Preferred, or take 50 flights. The points-earning bonus for those with that status goes from 100%, or double points earning, to 60% on qualifying flights.
- The new, top-tier Platinum status requires 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights. Platinum members will get a 120% earnings bonus on qualifying flights.
Silver status members will board in Group 1, while Gold members will board before Group 1. Platinum members will board before both Gold members and Group 1. Platinum tier also has unlimited Companion Pass trips.
Southwest's Companion Pass — which lets a designated person fly for free, minus taxes and fees, with a traveler who has that perk — is also changing.
Companion Pass holders that have them in their accounts will be able to hold onto them for the duration of their term. But starting with the 2027 earning year, Companion Pass benefits will be earned through TQPs or qualifying flights, by hitting a milestone reward or with Platinum status.
Currently, a Rapid Rewards member has to earn at least 135,000 qualifying points or 100 one-way flights to qualify for the pass.
The airline is also expanding its partnerships with international airlines and building its first airport lounges. Southwest on Thursday offered a peek into the new lounges, which it has named Icon, and is working on with its credit card partner, Chase. The carrier is building Icon lounges in four cities around the U.S., with others in the works.
Southwest is also adding benefits for customers that are in between status tiers, similar to what American Airlines offers.
For example, after earning 20,000 points or taking 15 qualifying flights, customers can choose between 2,000 more Rapid Rewards points or two coupons to select a "preferred" seat, which is a standard legroom seat that's closer to the front of the plane or a more popular aisle or window seat.
Customers will also get three Companion Pass trips after earning 95,000 points or taking 75 qualifying flights, which is below the Platinum threshold.
"That is definitely different from what we've done before," said Nandika Suri, who heads Southwest's Rapid Rewards loyalty program. She said the new strategy is "a way for us to actually recognize and reward customers ... faster and more frequently in their journey to continue to engage with us."
Airlines overall have consistently raised the requirements to earn status, requiring more spending, and have made similar changes to enter their airport lounges.
United Airlines on Tuesday said it would no longer allow customers to earn status in its Mileage Plus program based on flight segments next year and that it would only accept Premier qualifying points, which are earned from flight spending and on a co-branded credit card.
United also raised the requirements to reach Premier 1K, its highest frequent flyer tier outside of the invite-only Global Services, to 32,000 qualifying points, up from 28,000 this year.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this article.
